Issue Reading note
Two segment profit measures Uber reported Segment Adjusted EBITDA through FY2025 and Segment Operating Income from Q1 2026, recasting only 2025. For Mobility in Q2 2025 the two differ by $176M, 74bp of that quarter's Gross Bookings. A series that runs one measure to 2025 and the other from 2026 manufactures a margin step-down that did not happen, so the two are never joined here.
The revenue line breaks on 2 January 2026 UK Mobility moved from principal to agent, so Driver payments became a reduction of revenue instead of cost of revenue. Reported revenue declined $1.1bn in Q2 2026 and $2.1bn in H1 2026 with no effect on Gross Bookings and, by construction, none on volume. Growth rates, Revenue Margin and cost of revenue are not comparable across that boundary; Gross Bookings is, and is the denominator used throughout.
GAAP net income describes tax and equity marks FY2024 net income of $9,856M included a $6.4bn US valuation-allowance release against $2,799M of operating income; FY2025's $10,053M included a $5.0bn Netherlands release against $5,565M. Q2 2026 net income of $2,394M included $1.3bn of investment gains. Operating income and Adjusted EBITDA are the comparable lines.
The Mobility/Delivery volume split is estimated Uber reports Trips only as Mobility rides plus Delivery orders combined (13,567M in FY2025). Every per-trip and per-order figure here is derived from an assumed Delivery average order value, and two independent builds disagree by about a third on the Delivery order count. Growth rates are insensitive to the assumption; levels are not.

Uber reports no assets by segment, so no segment return on capital is computable from the filings. No sell-side research on Uber was available, so external expectations here are Bloomberg consensus plus cited press. Appendix C lists the external datasets that would test what Uber does not disclose.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Uber operates three marketplaces that share one app, one identity layer, one payments stack and one membership, and little else.▪ Mobility matches Riders with independent Drivers; Delivery matches Eaters with Merchants and Couriers; Freight matches Shippers with trucking Carriers. FY2025 revenue was $52,017M on $193,454M of Gross Bookings, a 26.9% Revenue Margin, and the three segments produced $11,438M of Segment Adjusted EBITDA before $2,708M of unallocated Corporate G&A and Platform R&D.

Segment FY2025 revenue ($M) % of total FY2023 YoY FY2024 YoY FY2025 YoY What it sells
Mobility 29,670 57.0% +42% +26% +18% Ride-hail across UberX, Comfort, Black, taxi, two- and three-wheel, carshare, rentals, transit ticketing and, from April 2026, parking
Delivery 17,248 33.2% +12% +13% +25% Restaurant delivery, Grocery & Retail, Uber Direct white-label logistics, and Delivery advertising
Freight 5,099 9.8% (24)% (2)% (1)% Digital truckload brokerage and managed transportation in North America and Europe
Total 52,017 100% +17% +18% +18%

(10-K FY2025 and FY2023, Note 13.) The revenue split and the economic weight differ. On Gross Bookings, Mobility was 50.4% and Delivery 47.0% of FY2025 volume, because Delivery is presented net in more markets; Freight was 2.6%, because Gross Bookings for that segment is defined as Freight revenue and not a transaction value.▪

The accounting customer differs by market, and the choice moves the revenue line without touching the economics. The 10-K: "Depending on the market where the trip is completed, the service fee is either a fixed percentage of the end-user fare or the difference between the amount paid by an end-user and the amount earned by Drivers" (10-K FY2025, Note 1). In the second set of markets Uber sells a fixed upfront price and buys a variable input priced on realised time and distance, so its cut on any single trip is a residual spread. PwC made principal-versus-agent presentation its first critical audit matter, against $46.9bn of FY2025 Mobility and Delivery revenue and $1.6bn of consumer discounts, promotions, credits and refunds paid to end-users who are not customers.

There is no backlog, no remaining performance obligation, no contract term and no escalator anywhere in the business. Uber elected the ASC 606 practical expedient because contracts have an original expected duration of one year or less; a contract exists only once a Merchant or Courier accepts a single transaction request. Every trip and every order is repriced.

Uber's own measurement of the US geography is that "only 30% of our U.S. gross bookings and 25% of our profits are coming from the top 20 cities" (Q2 2026 call), with 60% of Mobility Gross Bookings outside the United States (Q4 2025 call), against more than 8,000 US markets covering about 95% of the population [deck: Q4 2025 earnings supplement 2026-02-04, slide 9]. Uber also disclosed the demand variability underneath the autonomy argument: in the Austin AV operating zone "a typical Monday is ~45% of a Saturday while daily troughs are ~5% of peaks", and argues from those two ratios that "an AV only competitor must hold significant underutilized supply to match Uber's reliability and prices" [deck: Q4 2025 earnings supplement 2026-02-04, slide 8]. The ratios are disclosed; the conclusion is management's.

The premium and low-cost ends are quantified only in the decks. Low-cost products produce 75% higher frequency than standard-only users, premium products 3.5x the profit dollars, and together they drive more than 25% of first-time Mobility users [deck: Q1 2026 earnings supplement 2026-05-06, slide 7]. Mobility's non-ride adjacencies — carshare, rentals, transit ticketing, Uber for Business, Uber Health, driver financial products, and SpotHero parking, which brought $485M of goodwill into the segment in April 2026 — are named in the 10-K without a revenue figure, and they book at different values per transaction inside a per-trip denominator.

The three order-count angles span 50%: Delivery orders are somewhere between 25% and 34% of platform Trips. DoorDash's disclosed 3,172M FY2025 orders on $102.0bn of Marketplace Gross Order Value falls below the 3.4bn low end of that working band, so DoorDash's bookings lead is not evidence of an order-volume lead.

Advertising: Uber gives only the year-over-year dollar change: +$461M in FY2024, +$568M in FY2025, +$362M in H1 2026 and +$182M in Q2 2026. Two build-ups bracket the level. Rolling the February 2024 deck's "~$900M annualized revenue" at Q4 2023 forward by the two disclosed annual increments gives $1.73-1.83bn; two percent of FY2025 Delivery Gross Bookings is $1.82bn and two percent of the Q4 2025 quarter annualises to $2.03bn. Both anchors are softer than they look. The ~$900M figure was stated on the Q4 2023 call as company-wide advertising including Journey Ads, a Mobility format, and appears on a Delivery page only in the deck; and the "above 2%" penetration was an analyst's premise that management accepted qualitatively, and the quantified part of management's answer was "SMB ad penetration is a lot higher than 2%" (Q4 2025 call). Working figure: $1.7-2.0bn of FY2025 Delivery advertising revenue [estimate: run-rate build-forward from a company-wide Q4 2023 base plus disclosed Delivery-only increments, cross-checked against a stated penetration above 2% of Delivery Gross Bookings; the base's scope biases the level high], which is 10-12% of Delivery revenue and about 2 points of the 19.0% Revenue Margin.

That estimate decides how much of Delivery's profit is a marketplace and how much is a media business. Against $3,572M of FY2025 segment profit, $1.7-2.0bn at full flow-through is 48% to 56%.▪ The flow evidence is firmer than the level: the FY2025 advertising increase of $568M equals 52% of the $1,101M increase in Delivery Segment Adjusted EBITDA, the FY2024 increase of $461M equals 48% of that year's $965M, and the Q2 2026 increase of $182M equals 63% of the $289M increase in Segment Operating Income. Neither filing attributes segment profit growth to advertising in those terms — the 10-K says Delivery Adjusted EBITDA rose "primarily attributable to an increase in Delivery revenue including advertising, partially offset by a $1.6 billion increase in Courier payments" — and the 100% flow-through is an assumption. Instacart supplies the outside calibration: its FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of $1,087M and its advertising revenue of about $1,079M are the same number.

1.3 Freight

Uber Freight sells road capacity to shippers and buys it from independent carriers, recognising both brokerage and transportation-management revenue gross: "$5,099M of FY2025 Freight revenue is the amount billed to shippers, of which $4,583M was paid out to carriers." Payment terms run against Uber — shippers pay in 30 to 60 days and carriers are paid far faster — and a supplier-financing facility bridges it, with $2,358M of invoices confirmed during FY2025 against $2,326M paid.

1.4 What the three segments have in common

Capital intensity is close to nil today and the cost base is close to fully variable.▪ Consolidated purchases of property and equipment were $336M in FY2025, 0.65% of revenue and 0.17% of Gross Bookings, against $329M of depreciation, and $135M in H1 2026. The three cost lines that scale — Driver and Courier payments, trip insurance, payment card fees — move with volume; the fixed components are headcount, brand marketing and a technology stack shared across all three segments and reported in the unallocated bucket. Working capital runs slightly in Uber's favour in Mobility and against it in Freight; the balance-sheet item that dominates both is the insurance float, covered in Section 12.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Uber calls marketplace technology "the core of our deep technology advantage" (10-K FY2025, Item 1). Tested against what competitors have built and against what Uber buys instead of building, the claim holds for one layer and fails for several others.

Marketplace technology — demand prediction, matching, dispatch, dynamic pricing. The stack decides, for each request, which earner to assign, in what order, with what batching, at what price, and what arrival time to promise. The problem it solves is liquidity under variable demand: matching well across a 20x intraday swing is what lets Uber promise a short ETA without holding idle supply.▪ The February 2024 deck sizes the machine-learning layer at 10 million peak predictions per second and 20,000 models trained per month; Uber's own engineering documentation puts Michelangelo at over 400 active use cases and more than 15 million real-time predictions per second at peak (uber.com engineering blog, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The measurable outputs: three-quarters of Uber rides begin from a correctly pre-predicted destination suggestion with no typing (Q2 2026 call); AVs dispatched on Uber achieve about 30% higher trips per vehicle per day and about 25% faster ETAs than observed first-party deployments, on Uber's own estimate from CPUC filings and third-party data [deck: Q4 2025 earnings supplement 2026-02-04, slide 7]; and the AI cart builder produces carts "often twice the size" of non-AI carts.

What is not transferable is the trip history — 13,567M trips in FY2025 across more than 15,000 cities. The technique is published: Uber open-sourced H3, the hexagonal spatial index underneath its pricing and dispatch, in 2018, and Michelangelo's architecture is documented in detail. The scarce input is data volume and earner liquidity, not the algorithm.▪

Routing and mapping — bought, not built. Item 1 of the 10-K claims "We have built proprietary marketplace, routing, and payments technologies." Item 1A of the same filing states reliance on "Google Maps for the mapping function that is critical to the functionality of our platform" and that Uber does "not believe that an alternative mapping solution exists that can provide the global functionality that we require." That sentence is word-for-word identical in the FY2019 and FY2025 10-Ks, and the exhibit index tracks a Google Maps master agreement dated 29 October 2015, replaced in July 2020, amended in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Between FY2019 and FY2025 Uber spent $19,568M on research and development and did not displace the dependency.▪ The counterparty is Alphabet, which owns Waymo.

Payments. Uber Payments B.V. is an authorised electronic money institution in the EEA, with equivalent licences in the UK and Mexico. Over 75% of FY2025 Gross Bookings were paid by card or digital wallet. The barrier is the licence and the local method coverage, obtained jurisdiction by jurisdiction; the measured return is about 80bp of Gross Bookings taken out of the cost of payments between 2019 and 2023.

Uber One and the cross-platform stack. One membership spans Mobility, Delivery and Grocery & Retail: 46 million members at 31 December 2025 across more than 30 countries, over 50 million by Q1 2026, growing about 50% year on year and accounting for roughly half of platform Gross Bookings. About 40% of eligible members were active across both Mobility and Delivery in Q2 2026, with 400,000 participating merchants, up about 50% year on year, and merchant-funded offers up about 70% [deck: Q2 2026 earnings supplement 2026-08-05, slide 7]. The barrier is owning both a Mobility and a Delivery business at scale in the same market. DoorDash has DashPass and no ride-hail; Lyft has ride-hail and a far smaller delivery footprint.▪

Advertising. Journey Ads during the ride, sponsored listings in Eats, brand takeovers, car-top displays and in-car tablets. The scarce asset is inventory — a captive consumer during a ride and a purchase-intent surface in Eats — plus first-party transaction data. The serving technology is standard, and DoorDash and Instacart have built the same business on the same logic. In June 2026 Uber began selling its audiences off-platform through Google and Meta (marketingdive.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web].

Autonomy — integration and fleet operations. Uber does not build an AV stack. It sells four things to firms that do: demand, fleet operations, regulatory access and financing▪, packaged since 23 February 2026 as Uber Autonomous Solutions, with Uber AV Labs as the data arm fitting 500 Hyundai Ioniq 5 vehicles with 14 cameras, 8 solid-state lidars and 9 radars through NVIDIA's Drive Thor computer, targeting two million miles a month (techcrunch.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The Q2 2026 deck names 21 partners in three tiers: hardware platform (Lucid, Nissan, Verne, Volkswagen), self-driving technology (Avride, Baidu, Momenta, Motional, Nuro, Pony.ai, Waymo, Wayve, WeRide, Zoox) and fleet management (Avomo, Hertz, New Horizon, Otto, Rydera, SafeDriver ennoo, Tawasul).

Announced equity and milestone commitments to AV software partners total roughly $2bn on a press-tracker basis that mixes equity with commercial commitments, against the CFO's "$10 billion of AV investments … over a multiyear period" (techcrunch.com AV deal tracker, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The only AV commitment in the audited filings is the July 2025 agreement for Uber or its designated fleet operators to buy "a minimum of 20,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with Nuro's Level 4 autonomous driving systems over a six-year period", for which "as of December 31, 2025, our cash requirement has not been determined."

Three things work against the durability of this layer. The largest supplier is stepping back: Waymo service through Uber in Phoenix ended in mid-2026, and on 24 July 2026 the two ended exclusivity in Atlanta and Austin, with Waymo giving notice it will launch its own app in those cities in January 2028 and the existing contract running to May 2028 (cnbc.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The FY2024 10-K had already written the mechanism: partnerships "could expire" and partners "could … remove their vehicles from our platform." Second, scale: Waymo completed more than 500,000 paid rides a week across 14 US metros with over 4,000 vehicles as of September 2026 and targets one million a week by year end, of which Uber dispatches in two metros (startupfortune.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web], against Uber's entire global AV book of "hundreds of thousands of trips per week". Third, the fleet-operations layer is replicable by a smaller rival: Lyft's Flexdrive runs end-to-end fleet management for Waymo in Nashville from an 80,000 square foot depot, and there Waymo dispatches on its own app first.▪

Uber tried to build the stack and stopped. ATG was founded in 2015, reached over 1,000 employees and built more than 250 self-driving vehicles; it recorded Adjusted EBITDA losses of $537M, $499M and $375M across 2018-2020 against $142M of collaboration revenue from Toyota and DENSO, and was sold to Aurora in January 2021 with a concurrent $400M cash investment. That is Uber's own evidence on how hard the AV stack is.

Freight technology, the negative control. Uber Freight sells upfront transparent pricing, digital tendering and transportation management, and after nine years produced FY2025 revenue of $5,099M (−1%) at $(33)M of Segment Adjusted EBITDA and a $24M segment operating loss in Q2 2026. Four of the nine Freight competitors named in the FY2020 10-K (Convoy, Coyote, Transfix, NEXT Trucking) are gone from the FY2025 list, and Convoy, the best-capitalised digital native, shut down in 2023. The same marketplace stack pointed at a different two-sided market produced cumulative segment losses.

Research and development, and the 2026 inflection. GAAP R&D was $3,402M in FY2025, 6.5% of revenue, growing 9% against 18% revenue growth. The quarterly series says the full-year figure understates the run rate: R&D grew 13% in Q4 2025, 17% in Q1 2026 and 24% in Q2 2026, and 27% excluding stock compensation. Management named the cause on the Q1 2026 call: "when we set up budgets for 2026 in November, we underestimated the amount of impact the AI tools could have … So we've re-upped our investment here", offset against slower headcount growth, with "about 10% of our code now … built by agents."

Substitution. Two threats have no quantified answer. Agentic front-ends could intermediate the hail; the FY2025 10-K added a risk that "AI-enabled platforms and digital assistants, may disintermediate our relationship with consumers by controlling how our products are accessed", and Uber does not report the share of trips originating outside its own apps. And NVIDIA's DRIVE AGX Hyperion 10 reference architecture, announced October 2025, is designed to make any vehicle Level 4-ready and host any compatible software. If the stack commoditises on a merchant platform, the scarce assets become demand aggregation and fleet operations, which is exactly the layer Waymo has shown it can build and Lyft is already selling.

Where the differentiation is: Uber's durable assets are scale, local liquidity, brand, payments and transportation-network licences, and membership distribution. Technology converts those into service quality and the conversion is good. It does not by itself create them, and where technology would create a new business, in autonomy, Uber buys it from other firms.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

Uber discloses insurance expense only as a year-over-year change, and prior-year reserve development is recognised in current-year results. A meaningful share of the Q2 2026 Mobility margin gain came out of the cost line that contains insurance, and no disclosure separates an operating saving from a favourable reserve revision. Management describes the 2026 insurance relief as a rate-cycle event and the Mobility assessment takes it that way; it would be weaker if part of it were reserve development.

3.1 Mobility

Uber's Mobility advantage is real and earns returns well above its cost of capital, but it is a density-and-efficiency advantage and not a pricing one, and it is defensible for now while remaining open to erosion.▪

Uber's Mobility business has already been broken in three large regions by better-funded local rivals. Uber exited China in 2016, Southeast Asia in 2018 and Russia/CIS in 2018, converting operating businesses into minority stakes in Didi, Grab and the Yandex.Taxi joint venture, which the FY2019 10-K describes as "partnering with and investing in local ridesharing and meal delivery companies to participate in those markets rather than operate in those markets independently."

Scale has not bought a margin premium over smaller rivals in the same business. Uber Mobility earned 8.1% of Gross Bookings in FY2025 as Segment Adjusted EBITDA. Grab's Mobility segment, on the same pre-corporate-cost basis, earned 8.7% of GMV, $690M on $7,901M, a higher margin on roughly one-twelfth the volume.▪ Allocating Uber's unallocated corporate line by bookings share puts Uber Mobility at 6.7%. Uber's own February 2022 Investor Day set a long-term Mobility target of "over 10% of GBs and EBITDA margin"; four and a half years later, with Mobility Gross Bookings 2.7x the FY2021 level, the segment is at 8.1% on that measure and management no longer repeats the target.▪

Management is lowering realised price. Dara Khosrowshahi in September 2026: "we know there are fairly significant insurance tailwinds for us as it relates to cost that we're taking kind of reinvesting back into price and reducing pricing for consumers" (Goldman Sachs Communacopia, 2026-09-10). The economics come from taking unit cost out and converting it into volume, which is a cost-and-density advantage. It erodes once a rival reaches sufficient local density, and it is the advantage Uber's own 10-K declines to claim: "Although we may benefit from having larger scale and liquidity than some competitors, those network effects may not result in competitive advantages or may be overcome by smaller competitors. Maintaining a balance between supply and demand in any given area at any given time and our ability to execute operationally may be more important to service quality than the absolute size of the network."

The concession is that minimum efficient scale in Mobility is set at the level of a city at a time of day.

Management claims: the FY2025 10-K makes four hedged Mobility claims — a data and technical leadership claim ("we have the best technical and data platform to innovate faster"), a scale claim ("our scale and global availability allows our Mobility segment to offer better consumer experiences"), the marketplace-technology claim, and the cross-platform claim that dual-service consumers "generated over three times the Gross Bookings" of single-offering consumers while "only approximately one in five eligible consumers are currently active monthly across both of our businesses". On the calls management adds that it holds the majority category position in 10 of its top 10 Mobility markets (Communacopia, 2024-09-09, up from 8 of 10 a year earlier), and that membership is the defence: "member category position stays very, very consistent, while nonmember category position where consumers are more price sensitive … potentially go down" (Communacopia, 2026-09-10).

External sources: third-party card-panel work put Uber at roughly 71-76% of US rideshare spend against Lyft's 24-29% (secondmeasure.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web], a split that has been broadly stable for years while both companies' margins improved. Against that, Uber is buying a regulatory barrier it does not currently have: it is lobbying New Jersey and Washington D.C. lawmakers, alongside driver unions it litigated against for a decade, to require any platform offering self-driving rides to run a hybrid human-and-robot network, with the New Jersey proposal requiring human drivers behind at least 85% of rides during a three-year pilot (cnbc.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. A company seeking a statutory requirement that rivals keep human supply on the road is telling you the economic barrier is contested.

Ground-up view: Mobility is a matching business in which the driver supplies the vehicle, the fuel and the labour. The economics of any city are set by liquidity — enough drivers online that expected pickup time is short, enough riders that driver idle time is low — and that number is local and time-of-day specific. Once a rival has enough drivers in a given city at a given hour to hit a competitive ETA, the incremental value of Uber's global network to that city's rider is close to zero.▪ Brazil is the live demonstration: DiDi Food and Meituan entered the food business and bid up the two-wheeler supply Uber's Mobility business shares, and Uber's response was to move incentives from the consumer side to the supply side. Global scale did not prevent the local cost shock. Entry capital is small, since Uber's own capex is 0.6% of revenue; transportation-network regulations are compliance regimes open to all comers and not scarce licences; and switching costs are low on both sides, which the 10-K states outright.

Autonomy reverses that cost structure and management says so: "the majority of our cost today are variable … That model is changing pretty significantly as it relates to AVs because you go from a higher variable cost market model to a higher fixed cost model" (Communacopia, 2026-09-10). A fixed-cost, capital-heavy Mobility business has higher barriers to entry than the current one, and the party that owns the vehicles owns the operating leverage. Uber's claim to a share of it is the utilisation advantage, estimated at 30% from public data. Today AV is under 0.5% of trips, so Uber brings the scarce asset; when an AV operator reaches enough vehicles in a city to run its own liquidity, the demand Uber supplies becomes marginal and the take rate becomes negotiable.▪ Waymo's notice in Austin and Atlanta is the first real-world observation of that transition, and it came at the first sign of local AV density, before AV became material.

Return on invested capital. Segment assets are not reported, so return on capital can be computed only for the consolidated company.

NOPAT = income from operations × 0.76, a normalised 24% rate, because Uber's reported tax line is a benefit in FY2024 and FY2025 from valuation-allowance releases. Invested capital = receivables + prepaid + property and equipment + operating lease assets + intangibles + goodwill + other assets, less payables, accrued liabilities, lease liabilities and other long-term liabilities. Restricted cash, restricted investments and insurance reserves are excluded from both sides because the restricted pool collateralises the reserves; the $9,178M investment portfolio and net deferred tax assets are excluded as non-operating.

FY Income from operations ($M) NOPAT ($M) Invested capital, year-end ($M) ROIC on average capital
2022 (1,832) (1,392) 8,824 negative
2023 1,110 844 9,915 9.0%
2024 2,799 2,127 8,973 22.5%
2025 5,565 4,229 11,602 41.1%

Incremental return on invested capital between FY2024 and FY2025 was about 80%: NOPAT rose $2,102M on $2,629M of added capital. FY2025 free cash flow of $9,763M was 18.8% of revenue and 5.0% of Gross Bookings, and trailing-twelve-month free cash flow passed $10bn for the first time in Q2 2026. Against a cost of capital in the high single digits, these returns are high and rising. The denominator is small because the business needs almost no capital, and so does an entrant.▪

Versus peers, on margin over transaction value. Revenue is not comparable across these companies. Uber presents Mobility partly gross and partly net and has changed the basis twice in four years; DiDi recognises China ride-hailing gross; Grab recognises mobility net of driver earnings. Margin on gross transaction value is the like-for-like basis.

Four rows need qualification. Uber's Q2 2026 revenue growth of 12% against a latest-FY 18% is an accounting break and not a demand break: Gross Bookings grew 24% in the same quarter, and any margin-on-revenue comparison crossing 2 January 2026 is wrong by construction. Lyft's latest-FY row understates its current state, since FY2025 loss from operations was $(188.4)M while Q2 2026 GAAP operating margin was +2.6% with a record 3.2% Adjusted EBITDA margin on bookings. Bloomberg's ROIC is unusable for both Uber and Lyft because each released a large deferred-tax valuation allowance into net income, $6.4bn and $5.0bn for Uber and $2.9bn for Lyft. And Alphabet and Tesla are AV competitors and not economic comparables, since neither reports robotaxi separately. Bolt and Ola are private and file nothing, so their rows are empty.

The one-off compression in 2023 was Lyft's own turnaround. Since then Uber has added 1.2 points of fully-loaded margin and Lyft 1.3. On growth, Mobility Gross Bookings compounded 22.8% over 2022-2025 against Lyft's 15.4%, and in Q2 2026 the two were 22% and 22.6%, with Lyft's boosted by the Freenow and TBR acquisitions while its own Rides grew 11.8%. Against Grab the deficit narrowed and did not close, 6.3% to 8.1% against 7.2% to 8.7%; against DiDi the lead narrowed over FY2023-FY2025, 7.2% to 8.1% against 2.0% to 3.7%.

Analogues. The closest public comparison is Booking Holdings: a two-sided demand-aggregation marketplace whose supply side keeps a viable direct channel, where the advantage is consumer habit plus breadth of supply plus paid acquisition at a scale rivals cannot match, and which earns very high returns on a small capital base (FY2025 operating margin 32.8%, ROIC 51.8%, capex 1.2% of revenue). The comparison breaks on asset flexibility: a hotel room is fixed real estate that cannot be reallocated overnight, and an AV fleet is a programmable asset whose owner can route it to its own app in a single software release. Airbnb is the second analogue on the same habit-plus-local-supply shape, FY2025 operating margin 20.8% and ROIC 19.2%, with a structurally higher take rate and none of Uber's labour-classification or auto-insurance exposure. DoorDash is the nearest operating twin on earner supply and local density economics, at a FY2025 operating margin of 5.3% and ROIC of 6.3%, a band below. Uber Mobility is stronger than DoorDash on returns and weaker than Booking on durability.

3.2 Delivery

Uber Delivery earns an excess return on the bookings it processes and the gap over the delivery peers that disclose one has widened in each of the last four years.▪ The marketplace underneath that gap shows none of the marks of a durable advantage, and the advantage is open to erosion.

In FY2025 the segment converted 3.93% of its $90,864M of Gross Bookings into Segment Adjusted EBITDA. DoorDash converted 2.72% of Marketplace GOV, Delivery Hero's in-scope assets 2.62% of GMV, and Grab's Deliveries segment 2.26% of GMV in Q2 2026.▪ Four years earlier Uber Delivery was behind DoorDash on the same measure, −0.67% against +0.69% in FY2021.

The comparison is not presentation-neutral. Uber's Segment Adjusted EBITDA excludes the $2,708M Corporate G&A and Platform R&D bucket, while DoorDash defines Adjusted EBITDA from net income attributable to common stockholders and bears its entire corporate cost. And DoorDash's Marketplace GOV includes tips and membership fees while Uber's Gross Bookings exclude tips. Making both adjustments:

Basis Uber Delivery DoorDash
As printed, % of bookings 3.93% 2.72%
Uber fully loaded, corporate allocated three ways [estimate] 2.53-3.00% —
DoorDash restated to an ex-tips denominator at a 5-10% tip rate [estimate] — 2.87-3.03%
On revenue 20.7%, or 13.3-15.8% fully loaded 20.3%

On the like-for-like construction the headline 1.2-point advantage disappears, and on revenue the direction reverses.▪ Both adjustments are estimates and both are stated as bands.

Two assets produce almost all of the reported gap and only one has increasing returns. Advertising is roughly half of Delivery's profit on the estimate in §1.2, and it does have increasing returns, because the value of a purchase-intent audience rises with its size and with the number of merchant and consumer-goods advertisers bidding into it. Uber's advertising business is ahead of DoorDash's, which crossed a $1bn annualised run rate across DoorDash and Wolt only in 2024, and Uber's disclosed return on ad spend of more than 8x says the auction is not yet bid to equilibrium. Uber One is the second asset: 46 million members, over 50 million by Q1 2026, about half of platform bookings, and members spending 3x non-members.

The marketplace underneath shows the opposite. Realised price has not moved: the Delivery take rate was 19.5% in FY2022, 18.4% in FY2024, 19.0% in FY2025 and 19.1% in Q2 2026, and the CFO described the Q2 2026 revenue margin as "largely stable". Unit costs have not declined with volume: revenue less Platform Participant direct transaction costs was 56.3%, 59.3% and 58.9% of Delivery revenue in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 while bookings grew 43%. A fulfilment-scale advantage would show as that ratio improving with volume. Uber's own 10-K describes the industry as having "low barriers to entry, low switching costs" and consumers with "a propensity to shift to the lowest-cost or highest-quality provider", and merchants who "have a propensity to shift to the delivery platform that offers the lowest service fee". Category positions here have changed hands repeatedly and recently in both directions: Uber took the UK from third to first organically and launched Japan and Germany from scratch into leading positions, while DoorDash bought into Europe through Wolt and Deliveroo, Prosus consolidated Just Eat Takeaway and iFood, and Meituan and DiDi entered Brazil.

Meituan measures what a delivery network effect is worth against a determined attacker. It entered FY2025 as the Chinese category leader with an 11.0% consolidated operating margin. JD entered instant retail in February 2025 and Alibaba committed RMB 50bn of Taobao instant-retail subsidies in July 2025. Meituan's FY2025 revenue still grew 8.1% to RMB 364.9bn, and it recorded a net loss of RMB 23.4bn with core local commerce swinging from a RMB 52.4bn operating profit to a RMB 6.9bn loss (caixinglobal.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. That is a CNY 59bn swing, roughly $8.3bn at the 2025 average rate, against $8.7bn of combined FY2025 EBITDA for the five disclosed western and Southeast Asian delivery platforms. The capital that moved through one incumbent's segment profit in a single year is of the same order as the entire profit pool of the category outside China.▪

Where management's explanation does not hold. Management attributes the advantage to the cross-platform combination with Mobility: "a competitor who's mobility only or is delivery only structurally can't pay as much as we can and at the same time, we'll still have the same ROI as it relates to advertising" (Communacopia, 2026-09-10). Grab runs the identical structure — one app, mobility plus deliveries plus a paid membership plus advertising, in a single region — and its Deliveries segment earned 2.26% of GMV in Q2 2026, below DoorDash's pure-play 2.76%. The cross-platform combination on its own does not produce Uber's margin. What does is the advertising business that a large cross-platform consumer base makes possible at Uber's scale and that Grab is only now building▪, with 228,000 quarterly active self-serve advertisers at Q4 2025, up 21%.

The deck series also shows the acquisition-cost advantage narrowing in management's own numbers. At Q4 2021 the Uber Rides app acquired 2.1x the Delivery consumers of all paid channels combined at 25% of paid-channel cost [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 111]; by FY2023 the figure was 50% of paid-channel cost [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slide 9]; and in July 2026 it is restated as "more than 50% lower cost of incremental consumer acquisition compared to paid channels" [deck: M&A Announcement Delivery Hero 2026-07-16, slide 9], which is the same 50% expressed in a form that cannot get worse.

Membership Retention and renewal pricing holding or rising 46M to over 50M members, about half of bookings, 3x spend. The 10-K itself states "low switching costs" and every major rival runs an equivalent programme Real engagement effect, weak lock
Pricing power Realised price outrunning input cost Take rate 19.5% in FY2022 to 19.1% in Q2 2026; courier payments and incentives rose $1.6bn in FY2025 Not found
Advertising and data Monetisation rate rising with audience +$461M, +$568M and +$362M across FY2024, FY2025 and H1 2026; penetration above the old 2% ceiling; more than 8x return on ad spend Supported, and the strongest item in the list
Brand and distribution Organic category gains without subsidy UK third to first "all organic"; Japan number one; Germany from scratch to near-parity Supported, and simultaneously proof that incumbency here is takeable
Technology A capability rivals cannot copy Both Uber and DoorDash claim a unified stack, and DoorDash migrated Wolt and Deliveroo onto one Matched by rivals
Regulation Barriers that keep entrants out Delivery-specific regulation caps fees and does not restrict entry; DiDi, Meituan and JD entered new markets in 2025-2026 without licensing obstacles Not found

Where the evidence lands. Uber Delivery earns excess returns today and is defensible for now while open to erosion. It is not in the class of advantages that have already absorbed a well-funded attempt to break them and kept their pricing: no attack on that scale has been made on Uber Delivery, and the one time it was made on a comparable incumbent the incumbent lost its entire segment profit. Nor is it commodity economics, since 3.93% of bookings, a 20.7% Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin on revenue, and a gap over DoorDash that widened from −1.4 to +1.2 points in four years are excess returns by any definition.

Analogues. Maplebear (Instacart) is the closest public comparison and the match is nearly exact: a local-commerce marketplace whose fulfilment runs near breakeven and whose entire profit is retail media, with FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of $1,087M against about $1,079M of advertising revenue. It breaks on growth and breadth, since Instacart's GTV grew 11% against Uber Delivery's 22% and Instacart is one category in one country. Meituan is the structural twin — multi-category local commerce, an owned delivery network, membership, advertising and a mobility-adjacent business — and is also the downside case. Amazon's third-party marketplace plus retail media plus Prime has the same profit shape at far larger scale, but Amazon owns the fulfilment capital and Uber Delivery owns none.

3.3 Freight

Uber Freight does not hold a durable competitive advantage.▪

The segment lost $109M of Segment Operating Income in FY2025 on $5,099M of revenue against roughly $2.6bn of net assets inside Uber Freight Holding Corporation, a pre-tax return of about −4%. It is not a cycle artefact: Freight produced a negative Segment Adjusted EBITDA in seven of the eight years Uber has disclosed it, and the single exception printed at exactly zero.

In Q2 2026 Freight revenue grew $322M, or 26%, and Freight Carrier payments grew $320M. Net revenue went from $128M to $130M, a gain of 1.6% on a 26% revenue increase; across H1 2026 net revenue declined slightly, from $254M to $252M, while revenue grew 16%. Uber Freight does not set the spread between what a shipper pays and what a carrier is paid. The spot market does, and in an up-cycle the increase passes straight through.▪ RXO reported the identical pattern in the same quarter, with gross profit of $302M against $301M on 25% revenue growth.

Three claimed advantages hold on their own terms and still do not produce a return. Uber Freight has automated the load: segment operating expense outside carrier payments declined from $595M in FY2023 to $549M in FY2025 on flat revenue, and held at exactly $154M in both Q2 2025 and Q2 2026 while revenue grew 26%. The carrier network is real, with more than one million drivers onboarded, which Uber Freight puts at more than a quarter of all US truck drivers. And the technology claims are specific: 94% of loads auto-created, 100% auto-priced, 92% auto-booked [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slides 78-84], now with 30-plus AI agents on a book of more than $20bn of freight under management. What none of it buys is a wider spread. FY2025 net revenue of $516M was below FY2025 segment operating expense of $549M, and the difference is the whole Adjusted EBITDA loss. The business needs a net revenue margin of about 10.8% to cover its own cost base and earned 10.1%.▪

The industry structure explains why. Supply is atomised and multi-homes for free: the majority of US carriers are owner-operators with fewer than five trucks sitting on every load board simultaneously, and Uber's own risk factor concedes that "Shippers and Carriers have a propensity to shift to the platform with the best price and most convenient service." Demand is procured through annual routing-guide bids against five to fifteen other brokers. Entry cost is near zero against roughly 17,000 US brokers. The two places a real advantage could exist are cost per load, where Uber Freight has demonstrated one, and a shipper book with contractual stickiness, which is what it bought with Transplace and where the "over 95% customer retention" claim applies. Neither has been large enough to lift the segment above breakeven in four years.

Capital intensity runs against Uber Freight. It employs about $2.6bn of net assets against $5,099M of revenue, roughly 50%. C.H. Robinson employs $1,685M against $16,233M, roughly 10%, and earned a 4.9% operating margin and a 32.5% ROIC in FY2025.▪ The difference is $1,442M of Freight goodwill plus the Transplace intangibles, created by a $2.3bn all-cash purchase. Freight brokerage is a high-return activity for an operator that built its book; purchase accounting converted the same activity into a capital-heavy one for Uber.

Gap against C.H. Robinson FY2021 FY2023 FY2025 Direction
Operating margin, Uber best-case basis (6.1)% vs 4.7% = 10.8pt (1.2)% vs 2.9% = 4.1pt (0.6)% vs 4.9% = 5.5pt Narrowed, then widened
Net revenue margin, C.H. Robinson on its whole-company adjusted gross profit not disclosed 10.1% vs 14.8% = 4.7pt 10.1% vs 16.8% = 6.7pt Widening

The fraction of each freight dollar the intermediary keeps moved against Uber Freight.

Analogues. RXO is the near-exact comparison: a technology-forward truckload broker of similar revenue scale that lost $79M of operating income on $5,742M of FY2025 revenue, earned a −3.8% ROIC, and reported Q2 2026 gross profit of $302M against $301M a year earlier on 25% revenue growth. C.H. Robinson is the same moat shape, a matching intermediary between fragmented capacity and enterprise shippers, operating profitably at a 14.8% brokerage net revenue margin and a 32.5% ROIC; the analogue breaks on the balance sheet, because C.H. Robinson's advantage is a 120-year customer book and near-zero capital, neither of which Uber Freight can replicate by purchase. Landstar's agent-network brokerage earns a similar 12.4% net revenue margin on a comparably small capital base, with the caveat that its agent model is a different supply architecture.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Mobility

The ride-hail market is not one market. It is a set of city- and country-level duopolies or near-monopolies▪, and in New York City it is a statutory duopoly: the Taxi and Limousine Commission states that "the two companies currently licensed by TLC as HVs are Lyft and Uber" (NYC TLC, February 2026 For-Hire Vehicle License Review Report, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. Uber's FY2025 10-K names Bolt, Didi, Lyft and Ola as platform competitors, plus personal vehicle ownership, "which accounts for the majority of passenger miles in the markets that we serve", taxis, livery and public transport. It added Alphabet (Waymo), Amazon (Zoox) and Tesla to the Mobility competition paragraph for the first time in FY2025, and dropped Grab, which is consistent with Uber's absence from Southeast Asia since 2018.

Market sizing, built from each player's own disclosure.

Uber Mobility is 48.7% of the named five and 72.3% of the remainder excluding DiDi.▪ Neither is the true global share, because Gojek, Yandex Go, inDrive, Rapido, Ola, Cabify, Maxim and the Chinese platforms other than DiDi are not sized. The residual is most plausibly $30-50bn, which would put the global monetised pool at roughly $230-250bn and Uber at 39-42% [estimate: named-five bottom-up plus an unsized residual; the residual is the weakest input and the range travels with the number].

That $200bn is one to two orders of magnitude below the "multiple multi-trillion dollar markets" management uses, and Uber's own 10-K explains the gap, because most of that spend is personal vehicle ownership.▪ Uber has published one bounded version. Of its newer Mobility geographies — Germany, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Spain, Argentina — it said "these markets collectively spend close to $1 trillion on transportation each year … 2 years ago, we had $1 billion in gross bookings. And today, they're at $3 billion," which is 0.3% penetration of that particular trillion.

US share, derived. The CEO disclosed that "60% of our mobility gross bookings are international outside of the U.S." (Q4 2025 call), so US Mobility Gross Bookings are about $39.0bn for FY2025. Lyft's FY2025 Gross Bookings were $18,507M, of which the United States accounted for 95.9% of revenue; Freenow is a taxi aggregator whose bookings convert to revenue at a lower rate, so Lyft's US Gross Bookings fall in a $16.3-17.8bn band. That puts Uber at 68.7% to 70.5%, or 67.5% to 71.5% widening for rounding in the 60% figure [estimate: Uber's disclosed international share applied to disclosed Mobility Gross Bookings, against Lyft's disclosed bookings adjusted for its disclosed US revenue share]. Bloomberg Second Measure put Uber at 76% of observed US rideshare spending in March 2024, which is consumer card spend on a date 21 months earlier, so the two do not reconcile and neither establishes a trend.

Who is gaining. Q2 2026 was the first quarter in five years in which Lyft's bookings growth exceeded Uber Mobility's, 22.6% against 22.0%, and it followed a quarter in which Uber was 5.8 points ahead.▪ The convergence is mostly mix and acquisition: Lyft's Rides grew 11.8% while its bookings per ride rose 9.7%, and Q2 2026 includes Freenow, closed 31 July 2025, and TBR, closed October 2025, while Q2 2025 includes neither. On volume Uber is still growing about twice as fast. The direction still matters, because Lyft is no longer a purely North American operator and it entered Uber's fastest-growing region in the same year Bolt reached 850 cities.

Counter-evidence, most important first.

  • Waymo inside Uber's densest US metros. From a near-zero base to more than 500,000 paid rides a week across 14 cities in about two years, with a stated one-million-per-week target for end-2026. Uber's own FY2025 10-K added Waymo, Zoox and Tesla to the Mobility competition bullet, and its risk factors concede partners "could … remove their vehicles from our platform".
  • Lyft's entry into Europe through Freenow. Nine countries and 180-plus cities, in the region where Uber's revenue grew 65% over two years.
  • Bolt at scale and now profitable. €2.27bn of FY2025 revenue and a first annual operating profit of €19.5m after an €87.7m loss, so a competitor that no longer needs external funding to sustain price competition.
  • Uber's absence from China and Southeast Asia. Both its own decisions and both permanent on any reasonable horizon.
  • Regulatory pay floors and classification rulings. They set a minimum under the largest cost input.
  • Two-wheeler entrants in India. Price points a UberX-derived cost base does not reach [web, low confidence].
  • Public transport and private vehicle ownership, which the 10-K names.

One structural item runs the other way. New York's regulator reports that "over 800,000 Uber trip requests in Manhattan were forwarded to taxis" in the most recent month of e-hail request data, with more than 80% of all forwarded high-volume trips having Manhattan pickups [web]. Uber is monetising demand it does not supply, which extends its aggregation model onto the incumbent taxi fleet, and it also means reported high-volume trip counts understate Uber's demand capture.

Uber's last quantified category-position disclosure was February 2022: "over 80% of our current gross bookings are generated in markets where we have over a great 65% category position."▪ That figure is four and a half years old and predates the Waymo deployments, Bolt's expansion and Lyft's entry into Europe. Since then category position has been described only directionally, and the 10-K states that Uber tracks it "with internal systems and tools … that are not independently verified by any third party."

4.2 Delivery

Uber Delivery is the second-largest disclosed delivery marketplace by gross bookings and the most profitable of the five on bookings before corporate overhead.▪ DoorDash's Marketplace GOV passed Uber Delivery's Gross Bookings on as-reported definitions in 2023 and was $11.2bn, or 12%, larger in FY2025, but the two measures are not the same instrument, because DoorDash's includes consumer tips and membership fees and Uber's excludes tips. Restated to a common basis the crossover moves to 2024 or 2025 and the FY2025 gap narrows to roughly $1bn to $6bn.

The five barely overlap geographically: DoorDash is predominantly United States, Delivery Hero is MENA, APAC and Latin America, Instacart is United States grocery only, Grab is Southeast Asia. Measured across the disclosed pool the Herfindahl index is about 2,600, above the 1,800 threshold at which US agencies treat a market as highly concentrated; adding Prosus, Rappi, Gopuff, Swiggy, Coupang Eats and Amazon would push the pool above $340bn and the index toward roughly 2,200. Measured city by city it is a set of national near-monopolies: Meituan above 60% of Chinese food-delivery GTV, iFood above 80% in Brazil, Talabat above 50% in several Gulf markets, DoorDash the clear US restaurant leader with Uber Eats second, Instacart the US grocery leader with Uber holding five of the top ten US grocers as partners.

The platform layer keeps very little of the gross-bookings dollar. Adding the FY2025 profit of the five disclosed players gives $8.7bn on $299bn of bookings, 2.9%.▪ The remaining 97 cents go to merchants, couriers, payment processors and consumer discounts.

Uber ceded 8.1 percentage points of the two-player pool between 2021 and 2025; the annual loss decelerated from 4.1pp in 2022 to 0.6pp in 2024; and almost all of the 2025 loss is Deliveroo, since excluding it Uber's share slipped 0.3pp.▪ The 2026 quarters then reversed the direction organically, with Uber Delivery growing 26% in Q2 2026 against DoorDash's 23% excluding Deliveroo. Uber's take rate has been flat near 19% for four years while DoorDash's has risen every year from 11.3% to 13.5%, though part of the 5-6 point level gap is presentation and not economics.

Counter-evidence, most important first.

  • Meituan's Keeta. It took over 10% of Saudi share within months of its September 2024 launch and reached 33% by November 2025, launched in Dubai in September 2025 and Abu Dhabi in October 2025 against Talabat's above-50% position, and committed $1bn over five years to Brazil against iFood (techbuzzchina.substack.com and caixinglobal.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. Keeta is attacking exactly the two profit pools Uber is buying and defending, and Uber's CEO confirmed the Latin American pressure on the Q2 2026 call.
  • DoorDash's move from a single-country operator to a global one. Wolt in 2022, SevenRooms in 2025, and Deliveroo on 2 October 2025 for $3,724M, which brought the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Italy, Belgium, Hong Kong, Singapore and the UAE, all markets where Uber Eats competes directly, inside a competitor with $2.8bn of annual EBITDA to fund it.
  • Merchants in-sourcing. Uber Direct is the counter and neither side is sized.
  • Grocery. Uber is the challenger at roughly a third of Instacart's volume, and Instacart is the slowest grower in the set at +11%.
  • The AI-assistant disintermediation risk the FY2025 10-K added for the first time.

4.3 Freight

Uber Freight is the smallest of the eleven ranked North American brokerages by gross revenue and earns the thinnest spread among the nine of those eleven that report one.▪ Transport Topics ranks it eleventh on 2025 brokerage gross revenue of $2,040M against C.H. Robinson's NAST at $11,563M, Total Quality Logistics at $7,363M and RXO at $4,225M (ttnews.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web].

Total Quality Logistics runs hardest against the digital-brokerage case: privately held, a conventional carrier-sales model, and the widest spread on the list.

Market structure. Armstrong & Associates size the 2025 US Domestic Transportation Management market at $128,300M of gross revenue (3plogistics.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The eleven largest brokers account for $51,062M, 39.8% of that denominator, and contribute 198 Herfindahl points, far below the 1,500 threshold the Department of Justice treats as unconcentrated. The supply side is more fragmented still, with over 1.2 million active US motor carriers of which 97% run fewer than 20 trucks. Uber Freight's share of that denominator is 1.6% on the brokerage basis and 4.0% on the whole-segment basis, the latter overstated because the segment includes Europe and managed transportation.

Who sets price. Truckload capacity does, and in 2026 regulatory enforcement removed capacity. C.H. Robinson's own 10-Q: "Carrier capacity contracted further as regulatory enforcement activity impacting driver availability, combined with elevated operating costs, continued to strain capacity. These supply-side dynamics, rather than a meaningful recovery in underlying freight demand, remained the primary driver of higher transportation rates" (CHRW 10-Q 2026-Q2, Market Trends). Demand did not contribute, since the Cass Freight Index declined 3.3% year over year in Q2 2026. The mechanism is FMCSA non-domiciled commercial driving licence rules plus English-language-proficiency out-of-service enforcement, and the precise effective dates are not established in the trade coverage available [web]. Carrier cost rose faster than customer rate for the largest broker: C.H. Robinson's average truckload linehaul cost per mile excluding fuel rose approximately 29.0% in Q2 2026 against a customer rate up approximately 25.5%.

The competitor list Uber publishes: FY2019 through FY2022 named C.H. Robinson, Total Quality Logistics, XPO, Convoy, Echo Global Logistics, Coyote, Transfix, DHL and NEXT Trucking. FY2023 removed Convoy and Transfix; FY2024 removed Coyote and added RXO; FY2025 removed NEXT Trucking. Every venture-funded digital brokerage Uber listed alongside itself in 2019 is gone.▪ Convoy raised close to $1bn from Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, T. Rowe Price and CapitalG and shut down in October 2023, with Flexport buying its technology and none of its liabilities. The firms that survived and grew consolidated. RXO overtook Uber Freight in total revenue between FY2023 and FY2025 by buying Coyote Logistics from UPS at a final purchase price of $1,048M, closing 16 September 2024: Uber Freight was 34% larger than RXO in FY2023, 13% larger in FY2024 and 11% smaller in FY2025. Against the category leader Uber Freight has been flat, at 42.1%, 43.8% and 44.1% of C.H. Robinson NAST revenue across FY2023-FY2025 and 44.1% in Q2 2026.

Consolidated, the three segments earn 5.6 cents per dollar transacted before 1.9 cents of unallocated corporate cost, and Uber's non-GAAP operating income is 3.7 cents of every dollar that moves across the platform.▪

The split has barely moved since the IPO. Comparing FY2019 to FY2025 as a share of Gross Bookings, revenue rose 6.9 points and cost of revenue rose the same 6.9 points, because more markets moved to principal presentation, and the gross spread between them is identical in both years at 10.7%.▪ The entire swing to profitability came from Uber's own overheads and from the money it stopped spending to buy riders and drivers: sales and marketing declined 4.6 points of Gross Bookings, research and development 5.6, general and administrative 3.4, and operations and support 2.0. Excluding stock compensation from both years, the operating swing is 10.0 points, of which sales and marketing accounts for 4.6.

On the measure that nets earner payments out, Mobility's take was 20.7% of Gross Bookings in Q2 2026 against a disclosed Ridesharing Take Rate of 21% for 2018 in the IPO prospectus, on a definition that also netted Driver earnings and incentives out.▪ Eight years on, it is flat to marginally lower. The 20% figure sometimes quoted from the same document is the Core Platform blend of Ridesharing at 21% and Uber Eats at 10%.

Supplier layers. Earners are the largest input and the one Uber does not own. Uber's balance-sheet obligation to them at any moment is the $1,626M accrued Drivers and Merchants liability, about 0.8% of annual Gross Bookings and roughly three days of Mobility and Delivery volume, against $3,827M of receivables. Uber does not fund itself on earner payables, because Instant Pay removed that float.

Insurance is the supplier that mattered most and has stopped mattering, for now. Mobility insurance expense increases ran +$660M in FY2021, +$1.4bn in FY2022, +$1.4bn in FY2023, +$1.3bn in FY2024 and +$851M in FY2025, then +$45M in Q1 2026 attributed to miles driven alone with rate per mile no longer cited, and absent from the Q2 2026 cost drivers entirely. The CFO on the Q1 2026 call: "we expect to see hundreds of millions of dollars of savings in our insurance line this year … our auto insurance renewals that went into effect in March … we have found opportunities to also offload more risk to third-party carriers." Sizing the layer: FY2025 gross additions to insurance reserves were $4,879M, 5.0% of Mobility Gross Bookings, which matches the gap between Mobility's Other costs at 13.4% of its bookings and Delivery's at 7.2%, a business with far less auto liability [estimate: insurance is roughly 5-6 points of the Mobility dollar, from two independent routes].

Payments take roughly 1.3 cents of an incremental card-paid dollar [estimate: disclosed credit-card processing increases of $164M in Mobility and $124M in Delivery on $30,723M of incremental FY2025 bookings, and $130M plus $65M on $10,955M in Q2 2026, giving a 0.9%-1.8% band; the MD&A lists only material movers, so the low end understates]. Cloud and network commitments total $3.2bn of minimums, roughly 1.7% of one year's Gross Bookings. Apple and Google are named as a marketplace dependency, but rides and deliveries are paid on card-on-file, so the app-store fee does not apply to Gross Bookings.

Bargaining power, interface by interface.

Interface Evidence over five years Direction
Rider to Uber Insurance relief recycled into lower prices; 131bp of the Q2 2026 Mobility take-rate decline was deliberate investment in low-cost products; municipalities proposing take-rate and surge caps Toward the rider
Driver to Uber Earner-plus-tax share 74.6%-79.3% of the Mobility dollar in Q2 2026, against roughly 80% implied by the 2018 illustration; minimum-pay formulas in New York City and California; classification rulings live in seven jurisdictions Economics flat, legal basis moving toward the driver
Insurance carriers to Uber Four consecutive years of expense increases, then March 2026 renewals at improved rates and more risk offloaded to third-party carriers Decisively toward Uber after four years against
Merchants to Uber US marketplace fee schedule reset effective 11 March 2026: Lite 20%, Plus 25% with 30% on Uber One orders, pickup 7% with validated in-store pricing and 10% otherwise [web] Toward Uber, the first change in years
Carriers to Uber Freight Carrier share of the shipper dollar went 89.9% in FY2025 to 91.8% in Q2 2026 as the cycle turned Toward carriers
AV software to Uber Waymo gave notice around 24 July 2026 that it will launch its own app in Austin and Atlanta in January 2028, ending exclusivity; the existing contract runs to at least May 2028 Toward the AV stack
Card networks, cloud, app stores Over 75% of bookings on card; $3.2bn of cloud minimums; Apple and Google named as a dependency Static

The autonomous-vehicle chain Uber is assembling adds two layers below the demand layer that did not exist in 2024: financing, with Santander and unnamed third-party sponsors, and AV-specific insurance, with Marsh and Apollo, alongside the three partner tiers in Section 2. The economics of the layer depend on the AV software licence, which Uber, Waymo and Nuro all leave undisclosed, and Uber and Waymo are reported to share costs and revenue in Austin and Atlanta with the split confidential. Uber's answer is to fund the ecosystem so no single licensor holds the price, with ten named self-driving partners and a stated preference for breadth: "we want to make sure that we're not dependent on one partner" (CEO, Q2 2026 call).

Fleet-operator economics [estimate: at 25-32 trips per vehicle per day and $20-30 of Gross Bookings per US Mobility trip, one vehicle generates $183,000-$350,000 of annual Gross Bookings, midpoint about $265,000; after Uber's 25-30% revenue margin, $128,000-$263,000 is available to the OEM, the software licensor, the fleet operator and the insurer combined, against a $70,000-$80,000 Lucid vehicle, so supply-side revenue is 1.7x-3.5x the asset cost per year. The US Gross Bookings per trip input is not disclosed and is assumed].

Circular financing. Uber's chain now includes flows that make its supply depend on its own balance sheet. Purchases of non-marketable equity securities ran $52M in FY2023, $289M in FY2024 and $676M in FY2025, and the CFO states the leverage this creates: "for every dollar that we have invested, our partners have been able to raise an additional $2.50 from other investors." The Waabi investment secured exclusivity on the first 25,000 passenger vehicles Waabi produces. Unconsolidated variable interest entities are "primarily vehicle fleet operators", with total assets recognised rising from $678M to $1,329M and maximum exposure to loss from $803M to $1,509M during FY2025, including a term loan to Moove Cars Mobility that grew from $288M to $384M. And Delivery Hero has agreed to sell 14 markets with about $11bn of Gross Bookings to SSW Partners for about $1.6bn, concentrated in Delivery overlap markets and conditional on Uber's offer closing, with Uber lending SSW the majority of the purchase price, repayable over time including on a future sale [deck: M&A Announcement Delivery Hero 2026-07-16, slide 12].

The binding constraint has moved. Earner supply at an acceptable cost per trip was the binding constraint, and the cost side of it has released: Uber is passing the insurance saving straight through to price instead of banking it. Mobility Gross Bookings grew 22% in Q2 2026 while segment operating income margin on bookings rose only 36bp. Uber's behaviour implies that the binding constraint in 2026 is demand elasticity and not supply cost.▪ Lead times are short for human supply and long for AV supply — a 2026 production start, a six-year delivery window, city-by-city regulatory approval, and depot and charging build — so the constraint is migrating from a labour market Uber can clear with price to a capital and regulatory pipeline it cannot.

6. Secular and industry trends

6.1 Growth attribution: Uber's growth is volume, and always has been

Gross Bookings equal Trips multiplied by Gross Bookings per Trip, and both are disclosed annually.

2019 111 6,904 65,001 $9.41 +31% +32% (1.3)%
2020 93 5,025 57,897 $11.52 (11)% (27)% +22.4%

2022 131 7,642 115,395 $15.10 +28% +20% +6.4%

Window GB CAGR Trips CAGR MAPC CAGR GB per trip CAGR
