Of the six-year window's 19.9% Gross Bookings CAGR, 7.2 points a year come from Gross Bookings per Trip, and the whole of that gain was booked in 2020 and 2021, when Mobility collapsed and the mix swung to Delivery baskets several times the size of a ride fare. Strip the mix shift out and the price leg is negative: over FY2022-FY2025 Gross Bookings per Trip compounded at (1.9)% a year while trips compounded at 21.1%, the same shape as FY2017-FY2019. The durable driver is trip count, and trip count is consumers multiplied by frequency.▪

Frequency contributes almost nothing. Trips per MAPC per year went from 62.2 in FY2019 to 67.2 in FY2025, a 1.3% CAGR, and quarterly frequency growth disclosed on the supplemental deck ran +4%, +3%, +3% and +2% across Q3 2025 to Q2 2026. Management concedes it: "frequency, while it is growing at a slower rate, that is more a function of our cohorts coming on and maturing from there" (CFO, Q4 2025 call). Almost all of Uber's volume growth is new consumers.

Against industry dollars and against the peer cohort. No usable third-party market total exists: published 2025 estimates of global ride-hailing span $47.6bn, $49.7bn, $140.2bn, $163.6bn, $224.8bn and $284.7bn [web], and Uber's Mobility Gross Bookings alone were $97.5bn, larger than two of those six estimates of the entire world market. Any share claim built on a consultancy total is arithmetic on a number that differs across sources by a factor of six. The defensible denominator is the cohort of operators that publish a transaction metric.

Cohort Uber's FY2025 growth Cohort weighted growth Uber's share move [estimate]
Mobility and ride-hail: Uber, DiDi, Lyft, Grab +17.4% reported, +19% cc ~15.4% roughly 56% to 57%, range 55-58%
Delivery: Uber, DoorDash, Delivery Hero, Instacart, Grab +21.8% reported, +22% cc ~19.4% roughly 30.1% to 30.8%, range 30-31%

Uber grew about 2 points faster than the observable mobility cohort and gained about a point of it. In delivery it gained against the cohort average and lost against the largest single competitor: DoorDash's organic +23% against Uber's roughly +20% organic, after removing an estimated $1.3-1.9bn of Trendyol GO contribution, 1.7 to 2.5 points of the reported 21.8%.

Volume tells a different story from value inside the same cohorts. DiDi's China mobility orders grew 10.8% against GTV of +10.7%, so price per order was flat. Grab's mobility transactions grew 27% against GMV of +19%, so Grab cut price per trip by about 6% to buy volume. Lyft's rides grew 14% against bookings of +15%. Uber does not split Mobility trips from Delivery orders, so Mobility price per trip is not directly observable.

6.2 The 2026 inflection: volume decelerating, price and mix turning up

Quarter MAPC growth Trip growth Frequency growth GB growth reported GB growth cc
Q2 2025 +15% +18% +2% +17% +18%
Q3 2025 +17% +22% +4% +21% +21%
Q4 2025 +18% +22% +3% +22% +22%
Q1 2026 +17% +20% +3% +25% +21%
Q2 2026 +16% +18% +2% +24% +22%

Constant-currency Gross Bookings growth held at 21-22% across four quarters while trip growth decelerated from 22% to 18% and MAPC growth from 18% to 16%. The gap is Gross Bookings per Trip, which on the Mobility-plus-Delivery basis went from $13.92 in Q2 2025 to $14.60 in Q2 2026, up 4.9% as reported and about 3% excluding currency, after being approximately flat a year earlier at $13.99 in Q2 2024. Within a year the composition of Uber's growth changed: about four points of trip growth were replaced by about three points of price and mix plus two points of currency.▪

What plausibly drives the turn, from disclosed facts: the premium half of the barbell, with Reserve, Black and Uber for Business at +40% year over year in Q2 2026, airport XXL and shuttle; Grocery & Retail baskets at roughly a $15bn annual run rate; and Freight Gross Bookings, up 25% on a constant-currency basis, which generate no Trips at all. That ratio already excludes Freight, so Freight is not the cause. Cutting the other way, management says it is holding US prices flat or lower while reinvesting insurance savings, so if US pricing is flat to down while the blended ratio is up about 3% excluding currency, the up-mix outside the US and in premium and grocery products is larger than 3%.

6.3 Which legs are cyclical and which are secular

Spent. Airport trips were 11% of Mobility Gross Bookings in 2021 and 15% in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025, which is the pre-pandemic level, so the airport-recovery contribution is exhausted and anything further requires air-passenger growth at low single digits. Cash-paid trips were approximately 6% of global Gross Bookings in both 2023 and 2025 with card or wallet payment above 75%, so the emerging-market payment-digitisation leg is largely complete at the consolidated level.

Cyclical and currently favourable. The insurance rate cycle in US commercial auto is the most important cyclical fact in the current numbers and currently runs in Uber's favour. It is a rate cycle and not a structural change in Uber's cost base, and short- plus long-term insurance reserves still grew from $12,463M at December 2025 to $13,286M at June 2026, faster than Gross Bookings.

Cyclical and currently favourable for the wrong reason. Freight's 2026 acceleration is the truckload cycle. Freight Gross Bookings declined 25%, 2% and 1% on a constant-currency basis in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, then grew 25% in Q2 2026, while Segment Operating Loss was still $(24)M. US dry van spot rates were up 31% year over year in May 2026 and spot rates moved above contract rates for the first time in several years [web]. A brokerage whose revenue is a spread over carrier payments grows revenue with the rate cycle regardless of share, and it added roughly 0.7 points to consolidated Gross Bookings growth in Q2 2026 while adding no trips.

Unexhausted, each management-sourced and quantified.

Leg Disclosed position
US sparse and suburban markets Under 10% of eligible consumers in sparse markets used Uber in the past 12 months against over 50% in dense markets; sparse markets are about 20% of global Mobility trips, growing 1.5-2x dense markets
Cross-platform About 20% of consumers use both Mobility and Delivery, growing 1.5x faster than single-product users and generating over 3x the Gross Bookings
Membership 46M Uber One members at December 2025 growing faster than 50%, approaching half of Gross Bookings
Annual-to-monthly conversion 202M MAPCs against an annual active base "over 450 million"
Delivery selection "Our selection still in many countries is 30%, 40% of the addressable market"
Delivery advertising The prior 2%-of-bookings ceiling exceeded; +$568M in FY2025 and +$182M in Q2 2026

The cross-platform ratio has barely moved. About one in five eligible consumers is active monthly across both businesses today, and that figure has been quoted for several years.▪ Cross-platform use is management's most-repeated claim and its slowest-moving disclosed number.

6.4 Autonomy, and the arithmetic the 0.5% framing avoids

Uber had 7 live AV cities at Q2 2026 with 8 more launching by end-2026, and the CEO sized the volume: AVs complete "hundreds of thousands of trips per week" against about 300 million, "even less than 0.5% of our overall trip volume." That denominator includes Delivery orders and every international market. Autonomy competes in US ride-hail. Narrowing it:

  • Q2 2026 Mobility Gross Bookings were $28,988M; at 60% international, US Mobility Gross Bookings are about $11.6bn in the quarter.
  • At $22 to $30 per US Mobility trip, that is roughly 390M to 530M US trips a quarter, or 30M to 41M a week [estimate: the US average must exceed the $14.60 global Mobility-plus-Delivery blend by a wide margin because US fares include taxes, tolls and airport fees; the bounds bracket published US fare levels].
  • Waymo at 500,000 paid rides a week is therefore roughly 1.2% to 1.7% of Uber's US ride volume, against the 0.5% global figure management quotes.▪
  • Uber discloses that only about 30% of US Gross Bookings and 25% of US Mobility profit come from the top 20 cities, and Waymo's 14 cities are inside that set. Against roughly 9M to 12M Uber weekly trips in those cities, Waymo is running at roughly 4% to 6% [estimate: 30% of the US trip range above; dense-city fares run above the US average, so the true top-20 trip share is lower and this figure is conservative].
  • At Waymo's own one-million-per-week target for end-2026 those figures roughly double.

Waymo compounded tenfold in 22 months. Uber's US Mobility volume compounds in the high teens. On that arithmetic the crossover point in the top-20 US cities is not far out, and those are exactly the cities Waymo can serve first.▪

Uber's counter-position is breadth plus a commercialisation layer, and it has grown roughly sixfold in seven months: from a disclosed minimum of 20,000 Lucid vehicles with an undetermined cash requirement in the FY2025 10-K to "$10 billion of AV investments … over a multiyear period" and "120,000 vehicle commitments" on the Q2 2026 call. The 10-K states the funding consequence: "we may need to incur additional debt to finance the purchase of autonomous vehicles or infrastructure to support autonomous vehicles." Two management claims are checkable later and worth recording now: the 30% utilisation advantage over first-party platforms, and the $2.50 of partner capital catalysed per Uber dollar. The counter-evidence is in Uber's own risk factors, which concede that partnerships could expire, that partners could remove vehicles, and that Uber's AV investment "may add to Driver dissatisfaction over time, as it may reduce the need for Drivers."

6.5 Competitive pressure already in the volume line

Brazil is the live case and Uber describes it directly: "there is an enormous amount of competition as it relates to the food business. DiDi has introduced DiDi Food. Meituan has gone in there going against iFood … All of them are going after 2-wheeler delivery supply. And that same 2-wheeler delivery supply will switch off between delivering food and also moving people as well. So the cost of securing that supply has gone up pretty significantly … it is affecting trip volumes and it's actually competition outside of our space that is affecting those trip volumes" (CEO, Q2 2026 call). A delivery subsidy war raises Uber's Mobility supply cost and suppresses Uber's Mobility trips in the same market. It also shows that category position can hold while volumes decline, because the CEO said "we continue to hold our share in Brazil" in the same answer.

7. Critical points

1. The reported revenue line stopped describing the business on 2 January 2026, and the measure that replaces it shows a small margin gain. Mobility revenue grew 1% in Q2 2026 against Mobility Gross Bookings up 22%, because the UK moved to agent presentation and removed $1.1bn of revenue in the quarter. On the measure that survives the change — segment profit over Gross Bookings — Mobility went from 7.28% to 7.64%, 36 basis points, and Delivery from 3.52% to 3.84%. Consolidated non-GAAP operating income reached 3.7% of Gross Bookings against 3.3% a year earlier. Every growth rate, margin and take rate built on reported revenue breaks at that date.

2. Roughly half of Delivery's profit is a media business, and the level is an estimate. Advertising revenue growth equalled 52% of the FY2025 increase in Delivery Segment Adjusted EBITDA, 48% of FY2024's and 63% of the Q2 2026 increase in Segment Operating Income. The level is $1.7-2.0bn for FY2025 [estimate: §1.2] against $3,572M of segment profit, so 48-56% at full flow-through. Strip advertising out and the marketplace earned about $1.7bn on $90,864M of Gross Bookings, roughly 1.8%, and its take rate on orders declined about 110bp over two years. The estimate is biased high because the Q4 2023 base was company-wide advertising, and Uber discloses only the year-over-year change, so the level cannot be checked in any period.

3. Growth accelerated at a scale where the base rate says it should decay, and it did so on price and mix while volume slowed. Constant-currency Gross Bookings growth ran 18%, 21%, 22%, 21%, 22% across the five quarters to Q2 2026, against a cross-sectional base rate in which the median company at $40bn of revenue with a 22% trailing growth rate delivers 7.3% over the next three years. Underneath it, trip growth decelerated from 22% to 18% and MAPC growth from 18% to 16%, while Gross Bookings per trip turned from flat to about +3% excluding currency. The record says Uber's growth is volume; the current quarter is increasingly price and mix.

4. Free cash flow growth has separated from profit growth, and the cause is the insurance float decaying. FY2025 free cash flow of $9,763M grew 42%; H1 2026 free cash flow of $5,078M grew 7.5% while Adjusted EBITDA grew 34%. The accrued insurance reserve line contributed $2,660M of FY2025 operating cash flow, 26% of the total, and $830M in H1 2026, 16%. Claims paid grew 43% in FY2025 while additions grew 8.7%, so the two converge. Cumulatively, $8,539M of the $25,098M of free cash flow generated from FY2023 through H1 2026 is reserve accrual against claims not yet paid. Free cash flow conversion was 111.8% of Adjusted EBITDA in FY2025 and 95.8% in H1 2026, against management's 90% floor.

5. The largest capital commitment in Uber's history is announced on calls and absent from the commitment table. The FY2025 10-K discloses $2.4bn of non-cancelable commitments, of which $2.1bn is cloud, plus one AV commitment — a minimum of 20,000 Lucid vehicles with Nuro systems over six years — whose "cash requirement has not been determined." Six months later the CFO described "$10 billion of AV investments … over a multiyear period" and "120,000 vehicle commitments." The 120,000 figure spans all partners and is not stated to be Uber's capital; the CFO said "it's not just Uber's balance sheet that's working on this." FY2025 capex was $336M and consensus capex is $2,300M across four years.

6. The largest AV supplier is stepping back before AV is material. Waymo service through Uber in Phoenix ended in mid-2026, and on 24 July 2026 the two ended exclusivity in Austin and Atlanta with Waymo giving notice it will launch its own app there in January 2028, the Uber contract running to May 2028. Uber's own FY2024 10-K had written the mechanism a year earlier. The exposure today is small — AV is under 0.5% of platform trips and the top 20 US cities are about 30% of US Gross Bookings and 25% of US Mobility profit. The break came at the first sign of local AV density, which is what a bargaining-power model predicts.

7. Delivery Hero is a $13.7bn cash acquisition whose stated multiple depends on synergies larger than the target's entire profit. The deck's "~8x EV / 2027E Adj. EBITDA" is stated with the parenthetical "incl. Uber's existing economic ownership and over $1.2 billion of run-rate synergies". Delivery Hero's in-scope 2025 Adjusted EBITDA is about $1.1bn, so the synergy target is roughly 109% of the asset's current annual profit, and the CFO said the revenue-synergy component is "quite small relative to the $1.2 billion". On unadjusted 2025 in-scope figures the implied multiple is about 17x EV/Adjusted EBITDA and 0.45x gross bookings, at a 108% premium to the unaffected 8 May 2026 close. The timetable contradicts itself: over $1.2bn within 18 months of an H2 2027 close means April 2029, and the CFO said the primary platform migrations happen in 2029.

8. Uber reversed two doctrines within six months of each other. The company that sold China, Southeast Asia, Russia/CIS, Eats India, ATG and JUMP, exited Eats in eight countries and disposed of its entire Zomato position is now buying the largest cross-border delivery footprint available and committing its balance sheet to physical vehicle fleets. In the two quarters to 30 June 2026 it spent $617M on SpotHero, $2.3bn on additional Delivery Hero equity and $1.6bn on Delivery Hero total return swaps, drew a $2.0bn term loan, and then on 16 July launched a $14.8bn offer backed by a €14.2bn bridge. Its published capital-allocation framework now ranks autonomy second, above M&A and above buybacks, a line item that did not exist in February 2024.

9. Freight has never earned a segment profit in eight disclosed years, and the 2026 recovery reached its carriers. Cumulative Segment Adjusted EBITDA from FY2018 through FY2025 is $(847)M with a best year of exactly zero. In Q2 2026 revenue grew $322M and carrier payments grew $320M; across H1 2026, revenue grew $399M and carrier payments $400M, so the gross profit dollars Uber Freight kept declined while revenue grew 16%. Against roughly $2.6bn of net assets in Uber Freight Holding, the segment earns about −4% pre-tax, and its net revenue margin gap against C.H. Robinson widened from 4.7 points in FY2023 to 6.7 points in FY2025.

10. The market has de-rated the shares while the operating numbers accelerated, and the estimate line explains most of it. The shares declined 28.4% in the twelve months to 18 September 2026 while the twelve-month-forward consensus EPS rose 1.3% and the CY2027 EBITDA consensus rose 2.6%. Over the same twelve months CY2026 adjusted EPS consensus was cut 21.4% and CY2027 by 10.2%, entirely from items below EBIT: the ratio of consensus net income to consensus EBIT for CY2026 went from 100.2% to 77.9%. On EV/Gross Bookings, the one denominator untouched by the UK change, the tax releases and the equity marks, the market paid 0.71x at 22 September 2026 against 0.90x at FY2025 year-end and 0.98x at both FY2023 and FY2021.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"Mobility Segment Operating Income grew 28% on 1% revenue growth." True as printed and not an operating result. The 10-Q attributes the increase to higher Gross Bookings "and an $813 million decrease in Driver payments and incentives", and the same filing's cost-of-revenue discussion attributes $808M of that decrease to the UK business-model change. Taken literally, a presentation change that removes $1.1bn of revenue and about $0.81bn of cost reduces reported segment profit by roughly $292M. On the bookings basis, Mobility's margin went from 7.28% to 7.64%, 36 basis points, worth about $104M on the quarter's $28,988M of Gross Bookings, against an $851M annual insurance swing on the prior-year base. The UK change flattered the margin ratio on revenue and reduced the reported profit dollars.

"The net take rate is remaining broadly stable." The CFO asked investors to focus on the net take rate on the Q2 2026 call and described it as "largely show take rate remaining broadly stable". The same 10-Q's segment table gives 22.01% of Mobility Gross Bookings for Q2 2025 and 20.70% for Q2 2026, a 131bp decline worth $380M in the quarter and roughly $1.5bn annualised. He is internally consistent on the 400/100 basis-point split he gave a sentence earlier; "broadly stable" is not what the table shows.

"Delivery's revenue margin is largely stable." Reported Delivery Revenue Margin rose from 18.71% in H1 2025 to 19.29% in H1 2026, and Platform Participant direct transaction costs rose 59bp over the same half. Both statements hold at once, because the rise in the ratio is matched almost exactly by the rise in participant costs: Uber moved promotional spend from the consumer side to the courier side in response to two-wheeler supply competition, which raises the revenue margin and raises participant costs by the same amount with no change in economics. The higher revenue margin is promotional spend moved to the courier side.

"Delivery has a long runway to its top-ten-country margin benchmark." The February 2024 deck put Delivery at 2% of Gross Bookings against 7% for its top ten countries, with "Majority remain below best-in-class". The realised rate of improvement has roughly halved every two years: margin expansion on Gross Bookings was +222bp in FY2021, +166 in FY2022, +138 in FY2023, +95 in FY2024, +62 in FY2025 and +36bp annualised in H1 2026.▪ Realised incremental margin on incremental Gross Bookings declined from 21.8% in FY2022 to 6.8% in FY2025 and 5.1% in H1 2026 against an average margin of 3.8%, closing the gap between marginal and average from about 21 points to 1.3. The first four of those incremental figures are on the Segment Adjusted EBITDA basis and the last on Segment Operating Income, so the series is directionally right and not a single measure.

"Uber Delivery converts volume to profit better than DoorDash." True as printed at 3.93% of bookings against 2.72%, and it disappears on a like-for-like construction. Uber's segment measure excludes the $2,708M corporate bucket and DoorDash's Adjusted EBITDA bears its entire corporate cost; DoorDash's denominator includes tips and Uber's excludes them. Allocating Uber's corporate cost three ways gives 2.53-3.00% of bookings, and restating DoorDash's denominator for a 5-10% tip rate gives 2.87-3.03%. On revenue the direction reverses: 13.3-15.8% fully loaded against DoorDash's 20.3%.

"Uber is the demand layer autonomy has to come through." Uber's entire global AV network across 21 named partners runs "hundreds of thousands of trips per week", under 0.5% of platform trips. Waymo alone completed more than 500,000 paid rides a week across 14 US metros with over 4,000 vehicles as of September 2026, with Uber dispatching in two of them, and it targets one million a week by year end. Lyft's Flexdrive already supplies the same fleet-operations service to Waymo in Nashville from an 80,000 square foot depot, where Waymo dispatches on its own app first. And Uber is lobbying two US jurisdictions for hybrid-network mandates that would require any AV operator to also dispatch human drivers. The demand-layer claim has a real mechanism behind it: the disclosed Austin demand variability of a Monday at about 45% of a Saturday and troughs at about 5% of peaks. The conclusion drawn from those ratios is Uber's own.

"Management met or beat every leg of its three-year framework." Through two of the three years, yes. The February 2024 framework called for a mid-to-high-teens Gross Bookings CAGR, a high-30s-to-40% Adjusted EBITDA CAGR and 90%-plus annual free cash flow conversion, off an FY2023 base and running through FY2026.▪ Gross Bookings compounded 18.5% to FY2025, Adjusted EBITDA 46.8%, and conversion was 106% and 112%. The framework's own separately stated rule was Adjusted EBITDA growing at more than 2x Gross Bookings growth: realised 2.86x in 2024, 1.75x in 2025 and tracking about 1.45x in 2026. Management pre-announced that on the November 2025 call by replacing the multiple rule with a commitment to annual profit expansion "deliberately moderating pace of margin expansion." The prior framework, set in February 2022, missed its FY2024 Gross Bookings range of $165-175bn at $162,773M and beat its $5bn Adjusted EBITDA target at $6,484M.

"Uber guides conservatively and beats." On Adjusted EBITDA the beat has largely gone. The average outcome against the guidance midpoint was +24.5% across the nine quarters from Q4 2021 to Q4 2023 and +2.7% across the ten from Q1 2024 to Q2 2026. Five consecutive quarters from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 landed inside the guided range instead of above it, including Q2 2025 finishing $1m below the top of a $100m band. Gross Bookings has been steadier: 20 of 20 quarters at or above the low end, six above the high end, and an average of about one percentage point above the midpoint for five years.

"Capital return is policy at about half of free cash flow." It behaves as a residual. Uber repurchased $510M in Q2 2026, 18.3% of that quarter's free cash flow, against 56.6% in Q2 2025, and bought nothing at all in June 2026, a month before the Delivery Hero announcement and in the cheapest window of the year. About $4bn went into Delivery Hero stock and swaps in the same quarter. Four months earlier, on the Q4 2025 call, the company had said "our stock remains really cheap, we will continue to be aggressive buyers of our stock, and you should expect that it continues at a steady cadence." Asked directly on that same call whether the 50%-of-free-cash-flow commitment still held, management answered qualitatively and did not repeat the number; it was requantified on 5 August 2026 alongside the admission that Q2 had been diverted to M&A.

"Uber has never impaired a deal, so its M&A has been disciplined." Cumulative goodwill impairment since the IPO is $173M against $9,472M of goodwill at 30 June 2026, and that figure measures reporting-unit performance and not deal performance. Drizly cost $943M, generated $619M of goodwill and $395M of intangibles, and was closed at the end of March 2024; the FY2024 goodwill rollforward moved only $(85)M, all foreign-currency translation. Cornershop cost roughly $1.38bn and its app was sunset worldwide. Combined, about $2.3bn of purchase price for businesses that no longer exist, with no impairment recorded against either, because neither had its own reporting unit and both sat inside a Delivery segment whose profit was compounding.

"The 2016 and 2018 exits were the best capital allocation in the company's history." Uber recognised $6,219M of pre-tax gain on Uber China and about $2.3bn on Southeast Asia, $8.5bn in total, and the consideration was the buyers' equity. The Didi shares received at a $5,969M fair value were at $1,900M on 30 June 2026 and the Grab shares received at about $2.3bn were at $2,020M: roughly $8.2bn of value received now at $3,920M, with no shares sold in either. The disposals that produced cash were the smaller ones — Russia at about $1.7bn across 2021 and 2023, Zomato at $376M in Q3 2022, and Lion City Rentals at $310M in 2019.

"Insiders are buying." Three open-market purchases with no Rule 10b5-1 footnote total $16.9m: the CFO bought 22,453 shares at $71.25-$71.32 eight days after his appointment on 24 February 2026, the President and COO bought 70,000 at $75.23-$76.85 on 4 September 2026, and the CEO bought 141,000 at $70.73-$71.18 on 10 September 2026, after a 28.7% twelve-month decline. Against that, insider open-market sales across the same twenty months total roughly $73m, of which about $4.5m falls in 2026 — the Chief Corporate Affairs Officer sold 28,170 shares on 11 September 2026 and the Chief People Officer 30,000 on 16 March 2026, neither with a plan footnote. The CEO's own 450,000 shares sold in September 2025 at a weighted $97.07 were executed under a plan adopted 7 November 2024.

The five inflections

  • 2016-2018: exiting unwinnable geographies for equity in the winner. FY2016 Adjusted EBITDA was $(2,517)M on $19,236M of Gross Bookings at a (24)% Core Platform Contribution Margin; FY2018 was $(1,847)M on $49,799M at +9%. Gross Bookings grew 2.6x in two years while the EBITDA loss narrowed by $670M. Forced, because local competitors were better funded per market. What it reveals: Uber will trade operating control for a minority stake instead of funding an unwinnable local price war, and that portfolio then became a permanent feature of the income statement.
  • 2020: the pandemic and the amputation of optionality. Mobility Gross Bookings declined about 80% year over year in April 2020 and 73% in Q2 on a constant-currency basis, yet Mobility Segment Adjusted EBITDA stayed positive at $1,169M for the year and consolidated Adjusted EBITDA improved. Forced in timing, chosen in composition: the cuts landed on option value — autonomous vehicles, micromobility, sub-scale Eats geographies — and not on the two core marketplaces. What it reveals: the cost base is variable in fact, and what Uber sells first under stress is the assets whose payoff is furthest away.
  • 2022: from an EBITDA target to a free-cash-flow regime. FY2021 Adjusted EBITDA $(774)M and free cash flow $(743)M became FY2022's $1,713M and $390M, and FY2024's $6,484M and $6,895M. Chosen in direction, forced in urgency by rising rates. What it reveals: when Uber sets a paired volume and profit target, it delivers the profit leg and misses the volume leg.
  • February 2024: capital return, and the tax releases. Buyback authorisations went from $7.0bn to $27.0bn by July 2025, of which $6.5bn was executed in FY2025, and the diluted count declined from 2,125.6M in Q2 2025 to 2,050.2M in Q2 2026. Alongside it, two valuation-allowance releases turned GAAP net income into a figure governed by tax and equity marks.
  • 2026: both doctrines reversed. The asset-light doctrine and the exit-if-not-first doctrine were abandoned within six months of each other, with roughly $4bn of Delivery Hero stock and swaps bought in Q2 2026, a $14.8bn offer in July, and an AV programme sized at $10bn and 120,000 vehicles in August. The CFO: Uber "tactically pivoted quite heavily towards M&A in the second quarter."

What the record shows about the pattern

Under a demand shock Uber cuts optionality and protects the marketplaces. Under a competitive attack it cannot win locally it takes equity in the winner, and that portfolio moves GAAP net income by billions a quarter. Under a windfall it spends: FY2025 free cash flow of $9,763M and $19.2bn of remaining buyback authorisation were followed within two quarters by $4bn of Delivery Hero purchases, a $2.0bn term loan draw and a €14.2bn bridge commitment. Targets get reset instead of being missed in public: the FY2021 Adjusted EBITDA pledge of November 2019 became a quarter-end target during 2021, and the FY2024 Gross Bookings range of $165-175bn was missed at $162,773M without being discussed as a miss on the Q4 2024 call. And measurement changes cluster with strategy changes: the 2020 revenue-presentation restatement accompanied the pandemic reset, and the Q1 2026 switch to Segment Operating Income, the removal of Adjusted EBITDA from the 10-Q, the addition of Non-GAAP Operating Income to the release and the UK principal-to-agent change all landed in the same quarter as the pivot to large M&A.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

Person Role In role since At Uber since Before Uber
Dara Khosrowshahi, 56 CEO and director September 2017 September 2017 President and CEO, Expedia
Andrew Macdonald President and COO June 2025 2012 Bain & Company
Balaji Krishnamurthy CFO 16 February 2026 December 2020 VP equity research, Goldman Sachs
Jill Hazelbaker, 44 CMO and SVP, Public Affairs June 2019 2015 Snap; Google
Tony West, 60 SVP, Chief Legal Officer November 2017 November 2017 EVP and General Counsel, PepsiCo
Nikki Krishnamurthy, 54 SVP and Chief People Officer October 2018 October 2018 Chief People Officer, Expedia

The operating, legal, marketing and people functions are long-tenured; Khosrowshahi and West have both held their posts for nine years. The finance seat is the exception: three CFOs in eight years, with Nelson Chai from September 2018 to November 2023 (treated as an involuntary termination under the Executive Severance Plan), Prashanth Mahendra-Rajah for 27 months to 16 February 2026 with no reason given in the proxy, and Balaji Krishnamurthy from February 2026, who had not previously been a public-company CFO and answered the capital-allocation question on the Q4 2025 call twelve days before his appointment took effect. The board has ten nominees, with Ronald Sugar independent chairperson since July 2018.

10.2 What the plan pays for

CEO 2025 target total direct compensation was $30.3m: $1.1m of salary, raised 10% at the start of 2025 for the first time since 2017, a $2.2m target bonus at 200% of salary, and $27.0m of target equity, of which 77.5% was subject to performance or total-shareholder-return conditions. The annual bonus is 60% company financial goals (Gross Bookings, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA less stock compensation, 20% each) and 40% strategic priorities, with an individual modifier of 0.5x to 1.5x and a 200% cap. The 2025 performance share units were 40% Adjusted EBITDA Margin, 40% three-year average Gross Bookings growth, 10% electrification and 10% safety, multiplied by a relative total-shareholder-return modifier against the S&P 500 and capped at 150%.

The 2026 redesign changes both measures:

Plan element 2025 2026
Bonus, financial (60% of total) Gross Bookings 20%, Adjusted EBITDA 20%, Adjusted EBITDA less SBC 20% Non-GAAP EPS 30%, Gross Bookings 30%
PRSUs, financial Adjusted EBITDA Margin 40% (annual targets), Gross Bookings growth 40% (three-year) Non-GAAP Operating Income growth 45% (three-year), Gross Bookings growth 45% (three-year)
PRSUs, non-financial Electrification 10%, safety 10% Safety 10%
Equity plan evergreen Used every year since 2020 Waived for fiscal 2026, with no stated intent to use it again

Two features of the new measures matter. Non-GAAP Operating Income is defined in the Q2 2026 release as income from operations excluding only amortisation of acquired intangibles, legal and regulatory reserve movements, impairments, acquisition and financing expenses, restructuring, and other items not indicative of ongoing performance. It does not add back stock compensation or depreciation, and Non-GAAP EPS flows from it, so both 2026 financial measures are charged with stock compensation. And the long-term plan no longer contains a margin or efficiency measure: weight on growth measures inside the performance share units went from 40% to 90%, in the year immediately after the Adjusted EBITDA Margin metric paid 0% for 2025.

10.3 The payout distribution has no left tail

Year Company Goals component, % of target Completed PRSU cycle Payout
2021 120.00% 2021 PRSUs (FY21-FY23) 121.3%
2022 146.90% 2022 PRSUs (FY22-FY24) 150.0% (formula 158.9%, cut to the cap)
2023 158.74% 2023 PRSUs (FY23-FY25) 144.9% (111.5% on metrics × 1.30 rTSR)
2024 143.91%
2025 129.03%

Six completed cycles, six above-target outcomes, a five-year bonus mean of 139.7% and a three-cycle PRSU mean of 138.7%. The individual modifier has been applied above 1.0x once in five years and never below. Thresholds do bind when they are reached: the 2025 Adjusted EBITDA Margin tranche paid zero on a 14 basis-point miss (4.51% against a 4.65% target) and the committee did not override it. The payout curve on that metric is close to binary — a 3bp beat in 2024 produced 116.6% [estimate: (116.6% − 100%) ÷ 3bp from the disclosed 2024 target and result, implying roughly 5.5 percentage points of payout per basis point; the 2023 and 2025 points are consistent once the cap and threshold bind]. Across a 33bp band of a non-GAAP ratio Uber itself defines, the outcome moved from 150% to 0%. The committee also shortened a live performance period, measuring the diversity goals attached to the 2023 awards over two years instead of three.

CEO reported compensation was $24.2m in 2023, $39.4m in 2024 and $35.6m in 2025, against Compensation Actually Paid of $109.7m, $74.3m and $66.7m, which marks unvested equity to the share price. The CEO pay ratio for 2025 is 360 to 1 against a median employee total of $98,826.

10.4 What the metric set does not charge for

Every financial metric in both plans measures growth, margin or earnings. None applies a charge for capital employed, which matters more now than in 2022 because of what Uber is committing capital to: a minimum 20,000-vehicle purchase with an undetermined cash requirement, roughly $10bn of multi-year AV investment, and a $13.7bn cash acquisition backed by a €14.2bn bridge. Two design features interact with that. The proxies state that "Achievement of strategic goals may take into consideration the impact of certain M&A transactions", and that carve-out is written for the strategic goals and not for Gross Bookings growth or the operating-income measures. And Non-GAAP Operating Income excludes "acquisition, financing and divestitures related expenses" by definition. For the 2026-2028 performance cycle, acquired gross bookings count in full toward the 45% Gross Bookings growth metric while the deal and financing costs of acquiring them are excluded from the other 45% metric. Delivery Hero's in-scope 2025 gross merchandise value of about $42bn, or about $31bn after the SSW markets, is 16% to 22% of Uber's FY2025 Gross Bookings base, arriving inside the measurement window if the deal closes as guided.

Two of the five annual-bonus strategic priorities, together 16% of the bonus, are measured on data Uber produces itself: "Category position is based on internal estimates based on our billings and estimated billings of other rideshare platforms and/or food delivery platforms", and the culture goal is an internal twice-yearly survey. The committee has marked internal measures as failed before, grading the 2023 culture goal a miss.

A related-party structure worth recording: Turqi Alnowaiser joined the board in November 2023 and serves on the Audit Committee, which reviews related-person transactions. He is Deputy Governor and Head of the International Investments Division at the Public Investment Fund and has chaired Lucid Group's board since April 2023. The 72,846,072 shares attributed to him, 3.57% of Uber, are 72,840,541 held by PIF plus 5,531 held personally. Uber agreed in July 2025 to purchase, or have designated fleet operators purchase, a minimum of 20,000 Lucid vehicles over six years, and holds a Lucid equity position it marked down by $155M in FY2025. PIF's stake is below the 5% disclosure trigger, so the proxy's treatment is consistent with the policy as written.

10.5 Candor in the primary record

The profitability sequence was stated in advance and delivered: Adjusted EBITDA profitability, free cash flow positive in 2022, GAAP operating profit in 2023. Freight was promised a turn to profit twice — "a clear line of sight to EBITDA profitability" on the Q1 2021 call and "we expect Freight to generate positive adjusted EBITDA in 2022" on the Q4 2021 call, against $(74)M in FY2024, $(33)M in FY2025 and a $(24)M segment operating loss in Q2 2026. A long-term target stopped being discussed: on the Q4 2019 call the CFO said "long term, we remain confident about achieving our overall company adjusted EBITDA margin of 25% … we expect Rides to deliver adjusted EBITDA margin of 45% with a 25% take rate, and our Eats business to deliver adjusted EBITDA margin of 30% with a 15% take rate."▪ Those segment targets appear in no later transcript in the archive.

The sharpest reversal is on M&A. The CFO in October 2024: "we remain extraordinary disciplined … Uber's bar for M&A has never been higher. As Dara has said, the best deal is not having to do a deal at all and we are in that enviable position today." Twenty-one months later Uber announced a $14.8bn offer, after closing SpotHero, Getir, DanTaxi, Trendyol GO and Segments.ai. The framing changed as the CFO changed.

Management does answer hostile questions directly. On the Waymo dependency: "Waymo is a very, very important partner of ours… At the same time, we want to make sure that we're not dependent on one partner", followed by the scale check against its own bull case, "even less than 0.5% of our overall trip volume." On the Q1 2026 call the CFO conceded a planning error unprompted: "candidly, when we set up budgets for 2026 in November, we underestimated the amount of impact the AI tools could have." One claim has moved without a restated basis: the cross-platform multiple moved from "up to 3x" in February 2022 to "over three times" in the FY2025 10-K to "3 to 4x" on the July 2026 Delivery Hero call.

($M. The 2017 and 2018 buyback lines are pre-IPO private repurchases. FY2016 is absent because Uber's first 10-K presents FY2017-FY2019 only.) Uber has never declared or paid a dividend. FY2017-FY2021 consumed $13,351M of free cash flow; FY2022 was the first positive year at $390M; and everything Uber has ever returned to shareholders was generated in the ten quarters since Q1 2024, over which buybacks were 52.0% of free cash flow.

The buyback. Across the 24 disclosed months Uber paid a weighted-average $78.60 per share. An equal-dollar-per-month programme buying at each month's average price would have paid $77.05, so discretion cost about $1.55 a share, roughly $216M across the window [estimate: harmonic mean of the 24 monthly average prices paid, with June 2026 proxied at $71.65; the monthly average price paid is biased toward the days Uber transacted, so the figure is indicative]. The correlation between the month's average price paid and the month's dollar spend is +0.17 across the 23 months with purchases, so Uber spent more when the stock was more expensive. And the 144,395 thousand shares bought for $11,341M are worth $10,229M at the 21 September 2026 close of $70.84, a mark-to-market shortfall of $1,112M, or 9.8%; the FY2025 tranche alone, 79,978 thousand shares at $82.02, is 13.6% below.

Two decisions run in opposite directions. The January 2025 accelerated repurchase is the best-timed deployment in the record: 18,579 thousand shares at $66.59, eight months before the stock reached its high. Against that, purchases stopped entirely in June 2026 and totalled $510M for the whole quarter, in a window when the stock traded between roughly $68.85 and $76.20, the cheapest since early 2025.

What the buyback bought. Net issuance to employees was 54,601 thousand shares in 2024 and 39,354 thousand in 2025, so in 2025 employee issuance absorbed 49.2% of the 79,978 thousand shares repurchased: at the $82.02 average price, $3,228M of the $6,560M spent held the share count still and $3,332M shrank it. Shares outstanding rose 22.3% from February 2020 to the December 2024 peak, then declined 3.2% to 2,039,994 thousand at 30 June 2026. After $11.3bn of repurchases the count is still 18.3% above its first post-IPO disclosure.

Per share against enterprise.

Measure Absolute CAGR Per-share CAGR Leakage
Revenue, 2020-2025 36.1% 31.0% 5.1pp a year
Revenue, 2021-2025 31.4% 27.8% 3.6pp a year
Free cash flow, 2023-2025 70.4% 69.3% 1.1pp a year

Every year of operating leverage before 2025 came with share issuance that took three to five points a year off the per-share result. The leakage has narrowed to about one point since 2023.

What changed in the framework itself. The February 2024 deck's three-pillar policy was growth, liquidity at about 2x gross leverage, and return of excess capital with a bias toward repurchases. The July 2026 Delivery Hero deck restates it as a five-item ranking: invest in organic growth, invest in autonomous, pursue selective M&A, return excess capital, maintain investment-grade strength.▪ Autonomy did not exist as a pillar in February 2024 and now ranks second, above M&A and above buybacks, which makes buybacks the adjusting item.

What the free-cash-flow number leaves out: Insurance reserve accrual supplied 115%, 62%, 39%, 26% and 16% of operating cash flow across FY2022 to H1 2026, cumulatively $8,539M of the $25,098M of free cash flow generated from FY2023 through H1 2026; Uber's own February 2024 deck names it first among the drivers of conversion above 100% and states that the cash is "typically restricted, and not available for daily operations". Principal payments on finance leases of $157M in FY2025 are financing outflows and excluded from free cash flow, 47% of reported capex. And FY2025 working capital is not clean: the $2.2bn inflow includes the settlement of the Foodpanda Taiwan termination fee and a receivable recorded for non-income tax matters, principally the HMRC VAT assessments paid under protest.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Uber's acquisition outcomes split cleanly by whether the target sold the same thing Uber already sold. Every deal that bought more scale inside Mobility or Delivery is still inside a profitable segment with its goodwill intact: Careem, Postmates and Trendyol GO. Every deal that bought a different category has been closed, absorbed or left loss-making: JUMP was fully impaired in 2020 and the assets went to Lime; Drizly was shut down at the end of March 2024; Cornershop's app was sunset worldwide; Transplace is inside a Freight segment whose Adjusted EBITDA has been negative in three of the four full years since it closed. On top of that, the blocked Foodpanda Taiwan deal cost $236M in termination fees for no asset at all. Uber is a competent consolidator of its own two consumer categories and a poor buyer of adjacent ones. The pending Delivery Hero offer is the same-category kind of deal, which is the side of the ledger that has worked, but at $14.8bn of implied equity value it is larger than every prior acquisition combined and its stated multiple depends on synergies that exceed the target's entire current profit.

11.3 What the impairment record shows

Cumulative goodwill impairment since the IPO is $173M: $100M in 2020 (New Mobility, JUMP) and $73M in Mobility in 2021, with no reason given for the second. Goodwill went from $6,109M at December 2020 to $9,472M at June 2026, and the movements after 2021 are acquisitions, small divestitures and currency translation.

Three businesses stopped existing without a matching charge, and the mechanism is the reporting-unit test. JUMP had its own reporting unit, so the Q1 2020 test could fail and $100M went. Drizly and Cornershop did not; their goodwill went into the Delivery segment, which grew segment Adjusted EBITDA from $1,506M in 2023 to $3,572M in 2025, so no segment-level test could fail. About $2.3bn of purchase price disappeared into a growing segment's book value. Transplace is the live version of the same structure: $1,438M of Freight goodwill against a segment that lost money in 2023, 2024 and 2025 with revenue 27% below its 2022 peak, never reduced except by $8M of translation.

Share issuance for acquisitions in 2020-2021 totalled about 117.3 million shares, 6.00% of the 1,954,464,088 outstanding at February 2022: Postmates 70.4M, Cornershop 27.1M across two tranches, Drizly 18.9M and Routematch 0.9M.

11.4 Terms that changed, and regulator interventions

Foodpanda Taiwan was prohibited outright, and the FY2024 10-K contemplated settling the $236M fee either in cash or by returning the Delivery Hero shares Uber had bought in May 2024; the cash route was taken and the shares kept, which is why the $300M stake remained on the balance sheet and became the seed of the 2026 offer. Qatar blocked the Careem acquisition in that market in August 2019, and Morocco transferred only in September 2021. Mexico's regulator forced Cornershop to be split, with CS-Mexico held under a put/call for $94M until Mexican approval in December 2020. Postmates' consideration was a fixed 70,401,550 shares valued at $31.45 for an announced ~$2.65bn, and Uber's share price rose before the December 2020 close, so the recorded acquisition-date fair value was $3,902M, about 47% above the announced figure. Getir's price moved from $435M agreed to about $465M paid. And the Delivery Hero transaction was structured for clearance, with the 14-market SSW carve-out conditional on the Uber offer closing; the CFO's framing was "we've structured the transaction to facilitate the regulatory process."

The carve-out multiple is the clearest available evidence on what the overlap markets are worth without a buyer of scale: about $1.6bn for about $11bn of gross bookings is 0.15x, against the roughly 0.45x Uber is paying for the in-scope perimeter, and Uber is lending SSW the majority of the price.

Total at 30 June 2026 12,625 12,799 less $76M of discount and issuance costs, giving $12,723M on the balance sheet

There is no secured bank debt, but the stack is not uniformly unsecured: 61% of Uber's Aurora Class A holding was pledged as collateral at 30 June 2026, up from 48% at December 2025, and cannot be sold or transferred during the term of the 2028 Exchangeable Notes; and the 2029 Senior Notes are subsidiary-guaranteed, so they rank structurally ahead of everything else.

Three financings closed after the balance-sheet date. On 6 August 2026 a $7.7bn senior unsecured revolver maturing 2031 replaced the $5.0bn September 2024 facility, and a two-tranche euro Term Loan Credit Agreement for the Delivery Hero offer reduced the €14.2bn bridge by €4.0bn. On 15 September 2026 Uber settled a debut €4.5bn euro bond across five tranches — 3.750% due 2029 (€750M), 4.125% due 2032 (€1,000M), 4.375% due 2034 (€1,000M), 4.750% due 2038 (€1,000M) and 5.250% due 2046 (€750M), a 4.44% weighted coupon over 9.6 weighted years, with stated use of proceeds "for general corporate purposes". At €1.164 to the dollar those notes are $5,238M, taking pro-forma principal to $17,863M.

12.2 Weighted-average cost of debt

Principal-weighted stated coupon = sum of (principal × coupon) divided by total principal, on the 30 June 2026 stack. The effective rate adds discount and issuance-cost amortisation as disclosed instrument by instrument.

Basis Principal Rate
Stated coupon, whole stack $12,625M 3.69%
Effective rate, whole stack $12,625M 3.87%
Stated coupon, cash-pay instruments only $11,475M 4.06%
Stated coupon, excluding both 2028 equity-linked instruments $9,750M 4.62%
Stated coupon, straight fixed-rate senior notes only $7,750M 4.67%

Annual cash coupon on the 30 June 2026 stack is $466M; adding the euro notes takes it to about $699M, a blended 3.91% on $17,863M. The headline averages are depressed by the two 2028 instruments, $2,875M of principal or 22.8% of the stack paying 0.875% and 0.00%. Excluding them the stack pays 4.62%, which is where marginal issuance cost actually is, and the September 2026 euro curve priced Uber's own paper from 3.750% at three years to 5.250% at twenty, in the same band.

The refinancing step-up is concentrated entirely at 2028. Replacing the $1,725M convertible at 0.875% and the $1,150M exchangeable at 0.00% at roughly 4.2% adds about $105M of annual cash interest [estimate: $1,725M × (4.2% − 0.875%) plus $1,150M × 4.2%, using the 4.125% 2032 euro tranche as a six-year proxy], a 24% step-up on FY2025 interest expense of $440M from one maturity date. Both instruments settle against equity prices, so the cash requirement is not fixed: the convertible's conversion price is $72.54 against a $70.84 close, leaving it out of the money and repayable in cash, and the exchangeable's reference asset is Aurora Class A stock at an $8.50 exchange price with 61% of Uber's holding pledged and unsaleable until the notes are resolved. Uber's most recent term issuance is cheaper than its embedded average once the zero-coupon paper is excluded: in September 2025 it redeemed $1.2bn of 7.50% and 6.25% notes and issued $2.25bn at a weighted 4.51%, so principal rose $1.05bn while the annual coupon rose $17.8M.

12.4 Covenants and headroom

The senior note indentures contain customary incurrence covenants, and the 2028 convertible and exchangeable indentures contain no financial or operating covenants at all. The August 2026 agreements introduce the first financial maintenance covenant in Uber's capital structure: both the revolver and the Delivery Hero term loan require a ratio of consolidated adjusted EBITDA to consolidated interest expense of not less than 3.00 to 1.00, with cross-default and judgment-default thresholds of $500M.

Basis EBITDA Interest Coverage EBITDA that breaches
LTM June 2026, as reported $10,043M $462M 21.7x $1,386M
Pro forma for the euro notes $10,043M $699M 14.4x $2,096M
Pro forma with the full €10.2bn drawn at 3.5% $10,043M $1,115M 9.0x $3,343M

Even with every committed euro facility drawn, coverage is 3x the covenant, so the covenant is not the binding constraint on this balance sheet; the ratings are. Uber does not disclose them in any filing, but both August 2026 facilities price off them: Moody's Baa1 with a positive outlook since June 2025, S&P BBB+ since May 2026 and affirmed in July 2026 after the Delivery Hero announcement, Fitch BBB+ [web]. Moody's stated downgrade trigger is total debt to EBITDA sustained above 2.5x; Uber's own deck commits to gross leverage below 2x. The company's target and the agency's trigger are half a turn apart.

The deleveraging from 5.5x to 1.2x came entirely from the denominator: gross debt rose $1,239M over those three years while Adjusted EBITDA rose $7,017M. The direction has since flipped. Net debt more than doubled in the first half of 2026 without a single dollar of net issuance beyond the term loan: $2.3bn went to the additional Delivery Hero stake, $1.6bn to total return swaps on Delivery Hero stock, $653M to acquisitions and $3.5bn to buybacks, against $5.2bn of operating cash flow.

Liquidity after the August and September financings is about $19.0bn: $4,870M of cash plus $5,238M of euro proceeds plus $521M of short-term investments plus a $7,376M undrawn revolver and a $1,000M undrawn term-loan commitment. A $2.0bn short-term facility was drawn and repaid inside Q2 2026 under either the revolver or the commercial paper programme; both were at zero at 30 June 2026 and the filings do not say which.

The restricted balance sheet is larger than the debt stack.

($M.) Restricted assets grew from $2.4bn to $11.8bn in six and a half years, 2.2x the $5,391M of unrestricted cash and short-term investments and 93% of the entire debt stack. Insurance reserves of $13,286M exceed the $12,625M of debt principal and every other single liability line. Uber's own risk-factor language: "We also have requirements to post collateral for current and future claim settlement obligations with certain of our insurance carriers, which may have a significant impact on our unrestricted cash and cash equivalents available for general business purposes." The restricted portfolio is also what produces Uber's interest income, which was $743M in FY2025 and $740M over the trailing twelve months against $462M of interest expense, so Uber is currently a net interest earner by about $278M a year on float from the insurance book.

12.6 Leases, pension and purchase commitments

Operating lease liabilities were $2,008M at 30 June 2026, up $449M in six months after declining $70M through all of FY2025, because right-of-use assets obtained in exchange for lease obligations were $567M in H1 2026 against $126M for all of FY2025. Uber does not say what the new leases are for; acquired footprints and the AV depot and charging layer are both candidates. The weighted-average operating lease term is 15 years at a 6.6% discount rate, and a 100bp move changes the liability by roughly $130M [estimate: single-cash-flow duration approximation on $2,771M of undiscounted payments]. Finance leases are running off, from $310M to $222M in a year. Two 76-year Mission Bay land leases ending in 2092 have $1.7bn of future payments, 49% of it a financing obligation, with rent fixed through 2032 and then indexed to consumer prices, the balance sheet's only inflation-linked obligation, running 66 more years. There is no defined-benefit pension or post-retirement obligation. Non-cancelable purchase commitments were $2.4bn at December 2025, of which $2.1bn is cloud through November 2029, with a further $1.1bn minimum added in March 2026 through March 2031. The Lucid/Nuro vehicle commitment has no dollar attached.

Gross issuance has halved in three years, from 65,658 thousand in 2023 to 39,952 thousand in 2025 and an annualised 37,378 thousand in H1 2026, so the same repurchase dollars retire more net shares. Net dilution went negative in 2025 for the first time. The equity plan's evergreen — an automatic 1 January increase of up to 5% of shares outstanding under the 2019 Plan plus 1% under the employee purchase plan, about 124 million shares or 6.0% — was not used on 1 January 2026, and the company states it does not intend to use it again. What remains authorised is 633,627,571 shares available for future issuance, 30.6% of shares outstanding, plus 63,082,233 shares under outstanding options and rights at a $54.59 weighted exercise price. At FY2025 stock compensation of $1,826M and a $70.84 share price that reserve covers on the order of 25 years of grants [estimate: $1,826M ÷ $70.84 ≈ 25.8M share-equivalents a year against 633.6M authorised], so what limits dilution is the committee's grant practice and the buyback.

12.8 Structural balance-sheet risks, ranked by the size of a cash or earnings effect that could reasonably occur within 24 months

1. The Delivery Hero funding stack. The €14.2bn bridge of 16 July 2026 is about $16.5bn, 1.31x Uber's entire 30 June 2026 debt stack. €4.0bn has been termed out and €4.5bn of euro notes settled, leaving €10.2bn of bridge outstanding for roughly a year before an H2 2027 close, with commitment fees accruing from 13 November 2026. Uber guides gross leverage below 2x against a Moody's downgrade trigger of 2.5x. Holding under 2x with roughly $30bn of gross debt at close requires about $15bn of combined Adjusted EBITDA [estimate: $17,863M pro forma today plus €10.2bn drawn, against Uber's LTM $10,043M plus Delivery Hero's in-scope ~$1.1bn], roughly 35% above the current combined run-rate, and the gap closes through two more years of EBITDA growth, through cash funding part of the purchase, or through the SSW proceeds and Delivery Hero's own balance sheet.

2. Currency mismatch on euro-denominated liabilities. The bridge, the term loan and the €4.5bn of notes are all euro-denominated against a US dollar functional currency, and the euro earnings that would hedge them do not arrive until close. A 10% move on the €4.5bn actually issued is about $0.5bn, reaching about $1.7bn only if every committed euro facility is drawn. The September 8-K states the notes are for general corporate purposes, so the filings do not formally link them to the deal, and whether any part is designated as a net investment hedge is not yet on the record; the first reporting period containing them is Q3 2026.

3. Insurance collateral. $11,793M of restricted assets against $13,286M of reserves, growing with miles driven and insurance rate per mile. Reserves are actuarial estimates and a PwC critical audit matter; prior-year development runs through current-year results; Uber relies on "a limited number of ridesharing insurance providers"; and reinsurance and indemnification arrangements "transfer a significant portion of the risk from the insurance provider to us or our captive insurance subsidiary". A reserve strengthening or a collateral demand converts unrestricted cash into restricted cash without touching the debt stack. Lyft's Q4 2022 precedent is the mechanism at one-thirtieth the reserve scale: a $375M strengthening moved that quarter's reported adjusted EBITDA from +$126.7M to −$248.3M [web].

4. The 2028 maturity cliff. $2,875M of equity-linked paper at 0.875% and 0.00%, maturing within seven months of each other, adding about $105M of annual interest at the current curve, 24% of FY2025 interest expense, with the exchangeable's settlement dependent on Aurora's share price and 61% of Uber's holding pledged.

5. The €10.2bn bridge is not yet termed out and its margin is ratings-linked. A downgrade raises the margin on $7.7bn of revolver capacity and on the entire Delivery Hero term loan at the same time, in exactly the state of the world in which the deal is underperforming.

6. Floating-rate exposure, $2,000M at 30 June 2026, 15.8% of principal, rising materially once the EURIBOR-priced Delivery Hero term loan is drawn.

7. Structural subordination, narrow: the $1,500M of 2029 notes are subsidiary-guaranteed and rank ahead of $16,363M of pro-forma debt, and $1.9bn of the $4.9bn of cash at 30 June 2026 was held at foreign subsidiaries.

Covenant proximity is not on this list, at 21.7x coverage against a 3.00x test. And the HMRC VAT assessment of approximately $1.8bn has already been paid under protest and is held as a receivable, so an adverse outcome is a profit-and-loss and other-assets event and not a fresh liquidity call, except for the incremental assessments Uber says it expects.

13. Financial history and summary

Uber reports Trips only as Mobility rides plus Delivery orders combined, so every per-trip and per-order figure here is derived from an assumed Delivery average order value, and two independent builds disagree by about a third on the Delivery order level. The dollar and margin lines are disclosed; the unit lines are estimates.

The income-statement series uses the current revenue-presentation policy for every year. In Q4 2020 Uber moved cumulative payments to Drivers in excess of cumulative revenue from Drivers out of cost of revenue and into a reduction of revenue, and restated 2016 through 2019; FY2016 and FY2017 here are $507M and $530M below the revenue Uber published in its IPO prospectus, and FY2018 and FY2019 are $837M and $1,147M below the FY2019 10-K. Operating income, net income and EPS are unaffected in every year.

Forward columns are Bloomberg BEst consensus as of 22 September 2026. Four notes apply to that basis. The consensus operating-income line is the street's adjusted measure and ran about $837M above reported GAAP operating income for CY2025, the one closed year where both exist, so the 2026E growth cell is computed on the consensus series and not against the GAAP 2025 actual. Consensus gross profit and gross margin step up in 2026E because the UK principal-to-agent change moved Driver payments out of cost of revenue, not because of any margin improvement. Bloomberg publishes no consensus for operating cash flow, share repurchases, return on equity, return on invested capital or net debt, so those lines are blank in the forward columns; it does publish capex and free cash flow, which are shown. And ROIC is on the operating build defined in Section 3, excluding net deferred tax assets; including them the FY2025 figure is 22.3%, because the $8,560M average of deferred tax assets created by the two valuation-allowance releases was not funded by shareholders and generates no operating profit.

Revenue compounded at 35.7% a year from FY2016 to FY2025 and at 26.0% from FY2019. Gross Bookings compounded at 29.2% and 19.9% over the same spans, and the gap between the two is the revenue-presentation history and not a change in take economics. Interest coverage on Adjusted EBITDA over interest expense went 3.0x, 6.4x, 12.4x and 19.8x across FY2022-FY2025.

13.3 What the history shows

Growth is volume and the price leg is negative. Gross Bookings per trip peaked at $15.10 in FY2022 and has declined for three straight years to $14.26, 5.6% below the peak, while Adjusted EBITDA per trip rose from $0.22 to $0.64 over the same three years.▪ Profit per trip is expanding while price per trip is not.

The margin expansion has several causes. FY2025 income from operations rose $2,766M on $8,039M of incremental revenue, a 34.4% incremental operating margin, and the MD&A-sized drivers do not all point the same way. Cost of revenue rose $4,687M on Driver payments (+$1.6bn), Courier payments (+$1.6bn) and insurance (+$851M on rate per mile and miles driven). Sales and marketing rose $561M and research and development $293M, both on headcount and advertising. General and administrative declined $398M, mostly a $549M decline in legal-related accruals — which is the reversal of a $753M increase in the same line in FY2024, so about 20% of the FY2025 operating-income increase is litigation timing. In the opposite direction, insurance added $851M in FY2025 after adding $1,300M in FY2024, on inputs Uber does not set.

Operating leverage came from the lines below cost of revenue, and it has ended at the corporate line. The four operating expense lines below cost of revenue grew from $10,273M in FY2020 to $14,395M in FY2025, a 7.0% annual rate against Gross Bookings growth of 27.3% a year; measured from FY2019, operations and support grew 3.6% a year and sales and marketing 1.0% while Gross Bookings grew 19.9%. Corporate G&A and Platform R&D was $(2,353)M in FY2023 and $(2,410)M in FY2024, up 2.4%, then $(2,708)M in FY2025, up 12.4%, and $(2,180)M in H1 2026 against $(1,842)M, up 18.3%.▪ It is still growing slower than the 25% growth in H1 2026 Gross Bookings, and the near-flat corporate line that produced much of the FY2023-FY2024 margin expansion is gone.

Operating cash flow runs ahead of Adjusted EBITDA on insurance float. Accrued insurance reserves added $2,230M, $2,819M and $2,660M to operating cash flow in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, so about 26% of FY2025 operating cash flow is the build in claims not yet paid. Reserves reached $13,286M at 30 June 2026. Capex has run below 0.8% of revenue every year since FY2022 and below depreciation and amortisation every year since FY2021, so the reported asset base is shrinking in accounting terms while Gross Bookings compound at about 20%.

Segment mix. Delivery is converging on Mobility on both size and profitability. Delivery Gross Bookings were larger than Mobility's from FY2020 through FY2022; Mobility moved ahead by $5,171M in FY2023 and led by $8,410M in FY2024; the lead narrowed to $6,633M in FY2025 and $1,525M in Q2 2026. Delivery Gross Bookings grew faster than Mobility's in each of the last seven quarters, and Delivery Segment Operating Income as a share of its bookings rose from 3.29% in Q1 2025 to 3.84% in Q2 2026 while Mobility's went 7.49% to 7.64%.

Three inflections in the quarterly series qualify the FY2025 figures. Reported revenue growth decelerated from 20.1% in Q4 2025 to 14.5% and 12.2% in the two 2026 quarters, entirely the UK change; adding the disclosed impact back gives 23.2% and 20.9% consolidated, and 20.0% and 16.1% for Mobility against the reported 4.6% and 1.0%. Gross Bookings growth accelerated over the same period, from 13.7% in Q1 2025 to 25.5% and 24.1%. And free cash flow growth collapsed while profit growth did not: H1 2026 free cash flow grew 7.5% while income from operations grew 42% and Adjusted EBITDA grew about 33% in each quarter, because the accrued insurance reserve contribution went from $1,487M to $830M.

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

Management and the street agree on almost everything in the next four quarters, and past that the two publish different measures. Consensus is within 2% of every point of management's own Q3 2026 guidance, with 40 contributors agreeing on next quarter's EBITDA inside a $120M band on a $2.9bn number. Past that, Bloomberg publishes no consensus at all for Gross Bookings, Trips, MAPCs, Uber One members, Delivery advertising, insurance expense or any segment line, so the only drivers on which internal and external views can be compared are consolidated revenue, EBITDA and EPS.

Management and consensus disagree about capital. On revenue and EBITDA the two are within a few percent through CY2028. On the capital side, management describes about $10bn of autonomous-vehicle investment and access to more than 120,000 vehicles while consensus models $2,300M of cumulative capex across four years, and neither side has published a split between capitalised vehicles, equity in software partners and operating expense. Management says the intent is to keep the vehicles off Uber's balance sheet — "we are very, very actively also looking at financializing the ecosystem, and we are working with third-party financial sponsors" — and, asked directly how the $10bn flows through the income statement, the CFO said "we will give you more visibility into that as we go."

The second disagreement is about the acquisition. Uber's in-scope Delivery Hero perimeter is about $42bn of 2025 gross merchandise value, which at Uber's own FY2025 revenue margin would be roughly $8-11bn of revenue [estimate: in-scope GMV at Uber's revenue margin; Delivery Hero reports under IFRS on a different basis, so this is an order-of-magnitude figure]. The consensus revenue line contains no figure of that size, and the dispersion settles it: if part of the 36-contributor CY2028 cohort consolidated Delivery Hero and part did not, the standard deviation would be several multiples of the observed $3,165M.

How much to trust the internal numbers. Over twenty quarters from Q3 2021 to Q2 2026, Gross Bookings landed at or above the guided low end 20 times out of 20, six of them above the high end, averaging about one percentage point above the midpoint for five years. Adjusted EBITDA landed at or above the midpoint 20 times out of 20. But the magnitude has compressed by roughly nine-tenths: the average beat against the midpoint was +24.5% across Q4 2021 to Q4 2023 and +2.7% across Q1 2024 to Q2 2026, and five consecutive quarters from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 landed inside the range instead of above it. Two things changed at once in early 2024 and both point the same way: management moved to operating-income dollar growth as the primary internal metric and warned of "a little less acceleration", and the guidance bands narrowed in percentage terms as the base grew, from 6.2% wide on a $1.3bn EBITDA base in Q1 2024 to 3.6% wide on a $2.75bn base in Q2 2026.

Across the two multi-year frameworks the asymmetry is consistent: profit targets beaten, volume targets missed. The February 2022 framework targeted $165-175bn of FY2024 Gross Bookings against an actual $162,773M, and $5bn of Adjusted EBITDA against an actual $6,484M. Applying a uniform conservatism discount to management's numbers over-credits the top line.

The external view. Bloomberg lists 71 contributing houses, of which 58 publish a rating: 49 buy-equivalent, 8 hold, 1 sell, for a composite of 4.62 out of 5. Six are off the name, and the dates explain why: Deutsche Bank went restricted on 16 July 2026, the Delivery Hero announcement date; Morgan Stanley and Citi on 5 August 2026; JP Morgan on 6 August. Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America are the three institutions providing the committed bridge, and Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch International and BNP Paribas were representatives of the underwriters on the September euro notes. The published consensus for Uber is produced by the houses that are not working on its financing.

Where the street does disagree is with itself, and it widens with the horizon. Revenue dispersion goes from 0.8% of the mean for CY2026 across 49 contributors to 7.3% for CY2029 across 18; EPS dispersion from 5.7% to 15.0%; and the EPS mean falls from 0.8% below the median to 5.8% below it, so the minority publishing out-year numbers include a left tail that pulls the average below the typical analyst's figure. The mean target price is $101.88 against a $70.84 close, with a median of $100.00 across 56 targets dated in 2026 and an interquartile range of $90.00-$112.00. Only eight published targets are at or below $81, and the share price is inside that band.

GAAP diluted EPS is dominated by items below the operating line in four of the last five years, so the three multiple columns measure three different things. Twelve-month-forward P/E with the 24x median marked, and price-to-book on the right axis; prints before July 2023 are omitted because forward EPS below $1.00 produced meaningless values. Source: Bloomberg via xBBG, pulled 22 September 2026.

Price-to-book is recorded as description and not as a valuation basis, because Uber has not traded on book value and two deferred-tax releases moved the denominator far more than the price moved the numerator: book value per share went from $5.43 at FY2023 to $10.23 at FY2024, up 88%, while the price declined 2%, so price-to-book went from 11.3x to 5.9x without the market changing its mind about anything. The current 5.2x compares with a listed-life range of 1.7x to 15.0x.

Uber reports before the US open, so the reaction is the same-session close-to-close move.

The EPS basis breaks across the 2025/2026 boundary and any surprise series spanning it is measuring a definition change. Uber introduced Non-GAAP Operating Income, Non-GAAP Net Income and Non-GAAP EPS with the Q4 2025 release on 4 February 2026, recasting quarters back to Q1 2024. Its recast Non-GAAP EPS for Q2 and Q3 2025 is $0.60 and $0.65; Bloomberg's contemporaneous consensus for those quarters was $0.838 and $0.911, a basis on which Uber has never reported, and Bloomberg's own comparable-adjusted actuals were $0.637 and $0.683. Against the recast figures those prints are 28% misses; against Bloomberg's comparable actuals they are 24-25% misses. The shares moved −0.2% and −5.1%.

The next-quarter guide explains the reaction; the reported quarter does not.

The guide gap is small in every quarter, ranging from −0.94% to +1.70%. A difference of about one percent between the guided midpoint and what the street already held is associated with a 5% to 10% move in the shares.

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
Q1 2024, 2024-05-08 (5.7)% Gross Bookings of $37.65bn against a $37.93bn sell-side figure, and a GAAP net loss of $654m including a $721m net headwind from unrealized equity losses. Revenue and the Q2 guide were both in line (CNBC, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]
Q2 2024, 2024-08-06 +10.9% Adjusted EBITDA of $1,570m against a $1,504m consensus, GAAP EPS of $0.47 against roughly $0.31 expected. Q4 2025, 2026-02-04 (5.2)% Two items the same morning: a Q1 2026 non-GAAP EPS guide of $0.65-0.72 below the $0.75 street figure, and the CFO's departure on 16 February for a US government role (GuruFocus, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]
Q1 2026, 2026-05-06 +8.5% The Q2 EBITDA guide midpoint of $2,750m was 1.70% above the $2,704m already published, the widest positive gap in the window. Non-GAAP EPS of $0.72 beat, Gross Bookings grew 25%, Uber One passed 50 million members. Reported revenue missed by 1.0% on the UK change (Investing.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]
Q2 2026, 2026-08-05 (5.3)% The Q3 guide again: a $59.25bn bookings midpoint against a $59.33bn consensus, a non-GAAP EPS midpoint below the $0.89 estimate, and an EBITDA guide midpoint 0.57% below consensus. The quarter itself met expectations. The shares then recovered the entire move within three sessions, +3.4%, +6.5% and +4.0% to $78.03 on 10 August; Uber filed an 8-K on 7 August disclosing a €4bn term loan that reduced the Delivery Hero bridge commitment by the same amount, and no dated source attributes the recovery to it (CNBC, accessed 2026-09-22) [web, unverified]

Two quarters run against the pattern. Q4 2023 delivered adjusted EPS of $0.64 against a $0.26 consensus, a 146% beat, for a +0.3% move. Q3 2023 delivered $0.11 against $0.22, a 49% shortfall, and the shares rose 3.7% because Adjusted EBITDA beat and the Q4 guide midpoint was 1.1% above the published figure. Uber's EPS line is not what the market prices off.
