17. Forward model summary

The Delivery Hero block projects $14,700M of FY2028 revenue and $600M of operating income from Uber's own acquisition deck and the pending-acquisition note. Delivery Hero's net debt and any change-of-control terms on its convertible bonds are unknown.

The model is an operating model. It projects revenue through free cash flow and contains no valuation, no multiple, no target price and no discounting. Year 0 is FY2025; FY2026 is half reported.

17.1 What forces the construction

Gross Bookings is the forecasting denominator, not revenue. The UK principal-to-agent change removed $1.1bn of revenue in Q2 2026 and $2.1bn in H1 with no effect on Gross Bookings and no effect on profit, so every revenue-based growth rate and margin breaks across the 2025/2026 boundary while Gross Bookings does not. Each segment is built as units times price to Gross Bookings, cost ratios are applied on Gross Bookings, and revenue is an output.

The model runs entirely on the Segment Operating Income basis, anchored on the recast FY2025 figures of Mobility $7,207M, Delivery $3,153M and Freight $(109)M. On that basis the unallocated corporate line is $4,686M for FY2025, derived as the recast segment sum less consolidated income from operations, against the $2,708M Uber discloses on the retired Adjusted EBITDA basis. The new basis is 73% larger for the same year.

Non-operating income is set to zero in every year and every scenario, because FY2024 and FY2025 net income is dominated by two valuation-allowance releases and by marks on Didi, Grab, Aurora, Lucid and Delivery Hero, and Q2 2026 alone included a $1.1bn gain on moving Delivery Hero to equity-method accounting. Projected net income and EPS are therefore an operating result and will not match reported GAAP net income in any year in which a stake is remarked. Delivery Hero is a separate block outside the segment drivers, consolidating from FY2028.

17.2 Assumptions and where each is contested

Several assumptions do not survive their own evidence base.

Depreciation and amortisation at $1,570M in FY2033 is contradicted by the model's own capital plan. Base capex runs $600M, $1,050M, $1,450M, $1,700M, $1,800M, $1,900M and $2,000M across FY2027-FY2033, $10,500M cumulative, of which roughly $7,500M is vehicles, depots and charging. FY2029-FY2033 capex alone sums to $8,850M, which at a five-year blended life produces $1,770M a year of depreciation from those assets by themselves, before the pre-existing $719M base and before the SpotHero and Getir intangibles. Built by component — $3.75bn of vehicles at five years, $3.75bn of depots and charging at fifteen, $3.0bn of software at three — the figure is about $2.0bn before legacy assets. Recovering $1,570M requires a blended asset life of about twelve years across a robotaxi fleet completing mid-to-high-twenties trips per vehicle per day. The evidence supports $2.0-2.4bn, at or above the stated bear case, which would remove roughly $500-800M from FY2033 operating income and nothing from free cash flow.

Mobility Revenue Margin at 25.0% in FY2033 assumes no further principal-to-agent conversions, against a record of repeated conversions in both directions. The margin rose 760bp between FY2021 and FY2022 on UK business-model changes and driver-classification accruals, then declined 530bp between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026, of which the CFO attributes about 400bp to the January 2026 UK change alone. One market smaller than the US moved the ratio 400bp in a single step, which exceeds the entire 310bp bear-to-bull span assumed for eight years. Principal-versus-agent presentation is PwC's critical audit matter and driver-classification proceedings are live in seven jurisdictions, each of which would change presentation as well as cost. The defensible range is roughly 20% to 27%. The consolation is that the error is confined to reported revenue: a conversion moves revenue and cost of revenue equally and leaves Gross Bookings and segment operating income unchanged.

Gross Bookings per Mobility trip at +2.5% a year assumes a sign flip sustained for seven years. Platform Gross Bookings per Trip compounded at −1.9% a year over FY2022-FY2025 and declined in each of FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, with Mobility specifically running −1% to −2%. The +4-7% in Q2 2026 can be decomposed into about two points of currency, a composition effect from the low-fare Brazilian two-wheeler business slowing, and management's stated policy of holding US prices flat or lower. The evidence supports a base of +1.0% to +1.5% with a bear of −1.5% to −2.0%. At the sensitivity table's $4,468M per 1.5 percentage points, moving the base from +2.5% to +0.5% removes about $6.0bn of FY2033 operating income, 23% of the terminal figure.

The two Mobility cost assumptions are two sides of one decision and together assume the pass-through ratio halves. Q2 2026 removed 167bp of Other cost and returned 131bp of net take, a 78% pass-through; FY2025 removed 68bp and returned 39bp, 57%. The base removes a further 142bp of cost between Q2 2026 and FY2033 and returns only 55bp, 39%, and no disclosed period produces that. The Mobility Other cost assumption separately extrapolates one year of the insurance cycle over seven: the line improved 3bp between FY2023 and FY2024, 68bp in FY2025 and 167bp year over year in Q2 2026, and Uber's own pre-cycle measurement of structural leverage here was about 35bp a year. The evidence supports a Mobility net take nearer 19.5% with a bear below 18.0%, worth roughly $2.2bn of FY2033 operating income against the base, and a Mobility Other cost of 12.3-12.6% with a bear of 13.5-14.1%.

Corporate unallocated cost at $8,155M in FY2033 assumes an immediate two-thirds deceleration from the observed rate. The line was $4,686M in FY2025 and H1 2026 ran 18.2% above H1 2025; at that rate it reaches $7,600M by FY2029 and $13,900M by FY2033. The justification is the September 2026 reduction of about 3,300 roles, but the CEO said on 10 September that the savings would be reinvested in "lowering prices, improving selection", which lands in the Mobility take rate and not in this line. The evidence supports 9-10% a year, which still produces leverage against Gross Bookings compounding at 11.6%, with a bear of 13-15%. Three percentage points of growth on this line is $3,222M of FY2033 operating income.

Stock-based compensation at $3,140M in FY2033 continues a compression that has stopped. The ratio of stock compensation to revenue went from 6.7% in FY2021 to 3.5% in FY2025 and then flattened at 3.5% in H1 2026 once the UK revenue reduction is added back, while the base implies 2.6% by FY2033. The grant pipeline runs the other way: unamortised cost moved from $3.5bn to $4.9bn in six months over a 2.93-year recognition period, about $1.67bn a year of run-off from awards already granted; unvested units rose 25%; and FY2025 grant-date value of $2,737M grown at just 2% a year reaches $3,208M by FY2033 with no growth in the programme at all. The evidence supports $3.6-4.0bn, at or near the stated bear, worth $700-900M of FY2033 operating income and about $0.30 of EPS.

Several cash-flow assumptions are too narrow at the bear end. The insurance reserve build decays from $2,660M in FY2025 to $1,150M in FY2033 at about 5% a year after FY2026, against a decay already running much faster: the line annualises to $1,660M from H1 2026, a 38% drop in one year, and at the disclosed spread between claims paid growing 43% and additions growing 8.7% the two converge inside four years. The evidence supports $600-800M, and a bear of $(400)M to $0M, since reserves of $12,463M are actuarial estimates and a favourable year of prior-period development produces a net release. Cash taxes at $(5,700)M in FY2033 are roughly right at the midpoint and the $825M band is too narrow against three unquantified claims — the HMRC assessments, expected further assessments for 2023-2025, and driver-classification settlements in seven jurisdictions — so the bear belongs nearer $(7,500)M. Interest expense at $700M excludes the roughly $105M step-up from refinancing the two 2028 instruments, which takes the pro-forma figure above the stated bear of $800M. And interest income at $920M does not close against the balance sheet: base free cash flow runs $12.4bn to $24.4bn a year, the share-count path consumes about half, and Delivery Hero debt is only 28% repaid by FY2033, leaving $40-50bn cumulatively unallocated by then, which at 4% would earn $1.6-2.0bn by itself.

The Delivery Hero contribution of $2,600M in FY2033 is a top-quartile integration outcome against Uber's own base rate. Its only prior large acquisition failed on its own terms: Transplace closed in 2021 and FY2025 Freight revenue is 21% below the pro-forma combined base, with segment profit at or below zero in every year. The asset has never earned a group operating profit, at a −1.1% FY2025 operating margin on $15,893M of revenue after twelve years at scale, and the synergy timetable contradicts itself. All three scenarios assume the offer closes, though it is conditional on merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances in many jurisdictions and a 50%-plus-one-share minimum acceptance; the offsetting facts are Prosus's irrevocable commitment at about 17%, both boards' support, and Uber's existing roughly 37% economic exposure. The evidence supports $1.5-2.0bn with a bear at or near zero. The matching acquisition-debt interest of $530M is a principal-repayment range at a single fixed 4.5% rate, and a 200bp move in euro rates on $16bn is $320M, which puts FY2033 interest at about $1,040M, outside the stated bear by 44%.

Four assumptions that do survive their strongest attack are the Mobility trip path, the Delivery order path, Delivery advertising penetration and the Delivery Other cost line. Mobility trips at +9.0% a year is below the decay implied by extending the observed 2-points-a-year MAPC deceleration, and 60% of Mobility Gross Bookings is outside the US where no AV competitor operates. Delivery orders at +10.2% a year is below the midpoint of the +12-22% delivery base rate, and the subsidy-war attack lands on margin and not on volume, since Meituan's revenue still grew 8.3% in the year its segment swung to a loss. Delivery advertising penetration adds 16bp a year from FY2027 against a realised 45bp a year over FY2023-FY2025. And Delivery Other cost improves 11bp a year against a realised 60bp a year over FY2023-FY2025 and 36bp a year in H1 2026.

Bear and bull are deltas on these drivers. The bear case is built on Waymo compounding into the top-20 US cities, insurance reverting to rate-per-mile inflation after 2027, AV partners taking a larger share of the fare once supply is scarce, the Brazilian courier bidding war persisting and spreading, Delivery advertising plateauing below 3% as Amazon, Instacart and DoorDash compete for the same retail-media budgets, the truckload cycle turning, the AV financialisation failing so the vehicles land on Uber's balance sheet, the insurance float ceasing to fund cash flow, repurchase subordinated to deleveraging as it was in Q2 2026, and Delivery Hero delivering about a third of its synergy target late. The bull case is built on AV lowering cost per mile at roughly 1:1 fare elasticity, sparse markets converting from 10% toward the 50% dense-market penetration, Uber earning an AV commission at or above the human-trip take, Grocery & Retail and Uber Direct compounding, advertising advancing toward Uber's own 5% ads-plus-offers benchmark, AI coding tools holding headcount flat, third-party sponsors financing the entire AV fleet, and the full $1.2bn of Delivery Hero synergies landing by FY2029.

Mobility and consolidated stay below their historical best in every projected year. Delivery exceeds its most recent realised rate from FY2027, reversing a four-year decline from 21.8%, and the arithmetic behind the reversal is advertising: at 2.60% of Delivery Gross Bookings in FY2027 against 2.35% in FY2026, advertising adds $344M of revenue on $19,190M of incremental bookings with no marketplace cost against it, which is 1.8 of the 5.70 points. Removing the advertising step entirely takes the FY2027 incremental margin to about 3.9%, below H1 2026. The whole of the Delivery margin case is the advertising line, and the level of that line is an estimate Uber has never disclosed.▪

FY2026 reconciles against the reported half and the live guide: base Gross Bookings of $237,060M against H1 actual of $111,742M plus a Q3 of $59,903M against a guided $58.25-60.25bn; base revenue of $57,772M against consensus of $57,793M; base Adjusted EBITDA of $11,500M leaving Q4 at $3,290M, +32%, once the Q3 guidance midpoint is taken; base non-GAAP EPS of $3.32 against H1 actual of $1.53, a Q3 guide of $0.84-0.88 and consensus of $3.32.

Free cash flow conversion in the base case is 92.3% in FY2026, 87.3% in FY2027, 82.9% in FY2028 and 78.3% by FY2033, so it breaches management's 90% floor from FY2027 onward. Two disclosed mechanisms do it: the insurance reserve build decays from $2,660M to $1,150M, and cash taxes ramp as the $10,951M of net deferred tax assets is consumed.

The base share path requires retiring 68M to 102M shares a year after gross issuance held at 1.8% of the opening count. At a $75 average repurchase price that is $5.1bn-$7.6bn a year and at $110 it is $7.5bn-$11.2bn, against half of base free cash flow running $5.3bn in FY2026 to $12.2bn in FY2033. The path is affordable inside the stated policy at any repurchase price between $75 and $110 through FY2030.

18. Risks

Risks are ranked by the size of the exposure that can be quantified from disclosure, multiplied by how far the triggering event has already progressed.

1. The autonomous-vehicle partner layer proving rented. Mechanism: Uber supplies demand aggregation and ground operations to third-party AV stacks and takes a share of the fare; the counterparty owns the vehicle, the software and the safety record, and can serve the same rider directly. What has already happened: Waymo service through Uber in Phoenix ended in mid-2026; on 24 July 2026 the two ended exclusivity in Atlanta and Austin, with Waymo giving notice it will launch its own app there in January 2028 and the contract running to May 2028 [web]. Exposure: small near-term and bounded by geography. AVs are under 0.5% of platform trips; the top 20 US cities are about 30% of US Gross Bookings and about 25% of US Mobility profit, and 60% of Mobility Gross Bookings is outside the US, so the profit directly exposed to near-term AV deployment is in the low double digits as a share of group profit [estimate: 45.7% US revenue share times 25% of US profit in the top-20 markets, assuming profit mix tracks revenue mix, gives roughly 11%]. Leading indicators: whether the Austin and Atlanta Waymo fleets shrink before May 2028; whether a second partner gives notice; the count of exclusive AV cities each quarter; whether Uber discloses AV trips as a level. Mitigant: breadth. Uber names 21 partners across three tiers on the Q2 2026 deck. Management's own case for why pooled demand is worth something to a fleet owner is the disclosed Austin demand variability, a Monday at about 45% of a Saturday and troughs at about 5% of peaks.

2. The UK, where a $1.8bn receivable depends on a legal question a competitor has already lost. Mechanism: Uber UK became merchant of record on 14 March 2022 and remitted VAT on margin under the Tour Operators Margin Scheme. HMRC disputes that treatment and has assessed approximately $1.8bn (£1.4bn) for March 2022 to September 2024, which Uber paid to preserve the appeal and books as a receivable "because we believe that we will be successful in our appeal." The complication: both the FY2025 10-K and the 2026-Q2 10-Q state that "HMRC has expressed their intention to not enforce assessments pending the determination of the appeal of a competitor on a related matter." On 12 June 2026 the UK Court of Appeal allowed HMRC's appeal against Bolt and held that on-demand private-hire services do not fall within that scheme, reversing both lower tribunals, with a reported direct effect on Bolt of about £190m (matrixlaw.co.uk and vatcalc.com, accessed 2026-09-22) [web]. The 10-Q filed seven weeks later does not state the outcome or change the receivable treatment. Exposure: $1.8bn of receivable that becomes a charge if the treatment fails, plus additional assessments Uber says it expects for 2023-2025. The disclosed assessments cover 31 months at roughly $58M a month, so extending to the January 2026 cut-off adds about $0.9bn at a flat rate and up to $1.3bn scaled for UK volume growth [estimate], putting total UK VAT exposure in a $2.7-3.1bn range against FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of $8,730M. The 2026-Q2 MD&A separately opened a new, unsized VAT judgment risk on the post-January-2026 model. Why the UK matters beyond the tax: UK revenue was $10,609M in FY2025, 20.4% of group and second only to the United States at $23,771M, and three UK events land inside fifteen months: the January 2026 accounting change, the Bolt judgment, and DoorDash's arrival through Deliveroo [web].

3. The insurance book. Mechanism: Uber retains auto liability, uninsured and underinsured motorist, physical damage, general liability and workers' compensation risk through a wholly-owned captive. Reserves are actuarial estimates and a PwC critical audit matter, and three channels run off them — the expense line, the cash-flow line and the collateral line. Exposure: reserves grew 2.6x in three years, from $4,754M at the start of FY2023 to $12,463M at the end of FY2025 and $13,286M at 30 June 2026, and payments grew 43% in FY2025 against additions of 8.7%, moving the paid-to-incurred ratio from 38% to 50%. Prior-period development has been small so far — $158M adverse in FY2023, $78M and $21M favourable in FY2024 and FY2025 — but on a $12.5bn base a 5% adverse revision is $623M, 7.1% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA, and 10% is $1,246M, 14.3%. The reserve build supplied 27.2% of FY2025 free cash flow and 16.3% of H1 2026's. And $11.8bn of assets are already restricted against $5.4bn of unrestricted cash. Peer precedent: Lyft strengthened reserves by $375M in Q4 2022 and its reported adjusted EBITDA for that quarter moved from +$126.7M to −$248.3M [web]; Uber runs the same captive structure at roughly 30x the reserve scale. Leading indicators: the paid-to-incurred ratio in each Schedule II, the restricted-asset total each quarter, whether the accrued-insurance-reserve line in the cash-flow statement turns negative, and the prior-period development footnote. Offsetting: California's SB 371, effective 1 January 2026, cut the transportation-network uninsured-motorist requirement from $1,000,000 to $60,000 per person [web], and insurance was not named as a driver of the cost-of-revenue change in either 2026 quarter.

4. Delivery Hero: an 8x multiple that requires synergies larger than the target's profit. Terms: €41.50 per share, $14.8bn for 100% and $13.7bn net of prior purchases, minimum acceptance 50% plus one share, H2 2027 close, funded from cash plus new debt with a €14.2bn bridge, gross leverage guided below 2x. The multiple: the deck's ~8x includes both Uber's cheaper prior stake and over $1.2bn of run-rate synergies; on in-scope 2025 Adjusted EBITDA of about $1.1bn and an enterprise value of roughly $19.0bn less the $1.6bn of SSW proceeds, the pre-synergy multiple is about 16x [estimate]. The synergy target is 109% of the asset's current annual profit and the CFO said the revenue component is "quite small", so it is a cost programme worth more than the target's entire profit, executed on an IFRS reporter across 99 markets, with primary platform migrations scheduled for 2029 against an 18-month commitment that expires around April 2029. The position already on the books: 24.99% on the equity method at $3,502M against a disclosed fair value of $3.1bn, plus total return swaps bought for $1.6bn and carried at $1.5bn, so about $5.0bn of carrying value against about $4.6bn of market value, after a $1.1bn accounting gain was recognised in Q2 2026 on the transition. If the offer lapses, the deal premium in Delivery Hero's price goes with it. Inherited liability: Glovo, a Delivery Hero subsidiary, faced a €450m Spanish social security demand plus a €56.7m fine, disclosed reclassification contingencies in a €562m-€923m range, hired 14,000 riders as salaried employees by June 2025 and guided roughly €100m of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA impact [web]. That is the same classification mechanism at the top of Uber's own risk list, already crystallised in an asset Uber is buying. Leading indicators: the acceptance level at the end of the tender period, which merger-control authorities open a second phase, whether the bridge is termed out, any impairment of the $3,502M carrying value, and the SSW loan balance.

5. The autonomy capital commitment, announced on calls and absent from the commitment table. Mechanism: the FY2025 10-K discloses $2.4bn of non-cancelable purchase commitments and one AV commitment with an undetermined cash requirement. Six months later the CFO described $10bn of AV investment and 120,000 vehicle commitments. 120,000 vehicles at the $70,000-80,000 price the CEO cited for the Lucid vehicle is $8.4-9.6bn of vehicles alone [estimate: management's unit count times management's stated price range; the price was given for one vehicle type and the CEO separately described Rivian as "a very affordable bill of materials", so applying it across all partners is an upper reading], which would exhaust the $10bn before any equity investment. Uber's stated answer is third-party financing, and asked directly how the $10bn flows through the income statement the CFO said "we will give you more visibility into that as we go." Counterparty risk: the Lucid programme depends on a manufacturer whose new CEO is "refactoring the cost base of the business", backed by the Public Investment Fund, which is also a large Uber shareholder and holds Freight preferred stock. Leading indicators: whether a cash requirement appears in the FY2026 10-K commitments note, whether a fleet financing vehicle is announced and on whose balance sheet it sits, Lucid's production start against the 2026 target, and reported capex against $336M in FY2025.

6. Driver classification, now moving in Brazil. Mechanism: reclassification changes both the cost level and the financial-statement presentation, and the 10-Q says so: it "may impact our current financial statement presentation including revenue, cost of revenue, incentives and promotions." Live matters: a Brazilian Supreme Court case with a hearing expected in 2026 that "could use this case to provide broader guidance … potentially establishing a minimum baseline of rights, increasing our costs" — added in Q1 2026 and escalated in Q2 2026, two consecutive quarterly escalations; New Zealand's Supreme Court ruling of November 2025 that four drivers are employees while logged in; Mexico's December 2024 Federal Labor Law amendment; a pending French social-security assessment under appeal; Swiss and Netherlands rulings; Spanish food-delivery regulation presuming employment; the California Attorney General case still pending notwithstanding Proposition 22; more than 150,000 US drivers who have filed or signalled arbitration demands. Exposure: aggregate recorded liabilities for all legal, regulatory and non-income tax matters that were probable and estimable were $1.5bn at December 2024, $2.1bn at December 2025 and $1.8bn at June 2026, with no matter-by-matter accrual disclosed. Latin America revenue was $3,327M in FY2025, 6.4% of group, which bounds the direct Brazilian revenue at risk but not the precedent value. Independent mitigants: Proposition 22 was upheld by the California Supreme Court, the Massachusetts Attorney General case resolved in June 2024 with drivers remaining contractors, and two French Supreme Court decisions in July 2025 found drivers independent under the current model.

7. Competitive intensity showing up in volume before take rate. Mechanism: Uber's own 10-K describes low barriers to entry, low switching costs and consumers with a propensity to shift; the defence is cross-platform membership and multiproduct scale, and the cost of that defence is incentives and lower-priced products. What is happening now: trip growth decelerated across four quarters from 22% to 18%, monthly trips per MAPC growth halved from 4% to 2%, and MAPC growth went 17%, 18%, 17%, 16%, while constant-currency Gross Bookings growth held at 21-22%, so value per trip is doing more of the work. Q3 2026 guidance of 18-22% constant-currency bookings growth brackets Q2's 22% at the top and allows four points of deceleration at the bottom. Exposure: about 100bp of the 500bp Mobility revenue-margin decline is competitive spend, the balance being the UK change, which on Q2 2026 Mobility Gross Bookings annualises to roughly $1.2bn of revenue [estimate: 1.0% of $28,988M times four]. Leading indicators: trips per MAPC growth; the gap between Gross Bookings growth and trip growth; Delivery segment margin in Brazil-weighted quarters; whether Uber restates the "deliberate investment" framing as a competitive response.

8. Equity stakes swing reported earnings, and one is pledged. Investments of $8,759M plus equity-method holdings of $3,773M at 30 June 2026, $12.5bn of carrying value, move GAAP earnings by billions a quarter: FY2025 net income of $10,053M against $5,565M of operating income, and Q2 2026 net income of $2,394M including a $1.6bn pre-tax net benefit from revaluations against $17M of headwind a year earlier. Sixty-one percent of the Aurora Class A shares are pledged as collateral against the 2028 Exchangeable Notes and cannot be sold or transferred during their term.

9. Disclosure churn makes the operating record hard to follow. The segment profit measure changed in Q1 2026 with only 2025 recast; consolidated Adjusted EBITDA left the 10-Q; Non-GAAP Operating Income became the headline measure in the decks; the UK moved from principal to agent, breaking revenue, revenue margin and cost of revenue across the boundary; segment assets are not reported at all; and the CFO changed on 16 February 2026, announced the same morning as Q4 2025 results and five months before the largest acquisition in the company's history. The FY2025 10-K pre-announced part of this by adding ", or additional non-GAAP measures we introduce" to the list of things that can move the share price.

10. Freight. Still a reportable segment in every 2026 filing and still loss-making at $(24)M of segment operating income in Q2 2026 despite revenue +26%. Freight Holding is a consolidated variable interest entity with $3.5bn of assets and $939M of liabilities at 30 June 2026, holds preferred stock with liquidation preferences and 6% cumulative dividends, and had minority common holders with put rights that a majority exercised in Q3 2025.

Which risks arrive together. Three clusters matter more than any single item. The UK cluster: an adverse HMRC outcome, a challenge to the post-January-2026 model, and DoorDash-owned Deliveroo taking UK Delivery share all hit the same 20.4% of FY2025 revenue, and the accounting change has already removed $2.1bn of reported H1 2026 revenue from that geography, so a share loss there is harder to see in the reported series. The capital cluster: Delivery Hero requires $13.7bn of cash by H2 2027 against $5.4bn of unrestricted cash and short-term investments at 30 June 2026; the AV programme requires up to $10bn over a similar horizon; and $15.7bn of buyback authorisation remains. These draw on the same balance sheet, and the flex line has already moved — Q2 2026 repurchases were $510M against $1.4bn a year earlier, with nothing at all in June 2026. The insurance-and-cash cluster: adverse reserve development raises the expense line, shrinks the reserve-build contribution to operating cash flow, and increases the collateral Uber must post, all in the same period.

Analyst questions have moved. Counting theme mentions in the Q&A section of each earnings call, autonomy went from absent before 2024 to 34-55 mentions a quarter from Q3 2024 onward and has stayed there; insurance spikes in exactly the quarters where the expense inflected; take rate returned in Q2 2026 because of the UK change; and Delivery Hero went from 0-4 mentions to 15 in Q2 2026. Five questions were deflected or answered with a forward promise: the operational-versus-revenue synergy split on the Delivery Hero call ("I'm not going to get into that level of granularity"), the $10bn AV programme's income-statement path ("we will give you more visibility into that as we go"), the Waymo relationship, Mobility cohort behaviour in markets where a competing AV product is live and not on Uber, and personal AI agents abstracting the Uber app away from the consumer.

19. Source disclosure

Primary filings. Seven annual reports (FY2019-FY2025), the IPO S-1 and 424B4 prospectus, six quarterly reports (2024-Q3, 2025-Q1 through 2025-Q3, 2026-Q1 and 2026-Q2), four 8-Ks pulled specifically for this work covering the July 2026 Delivery Hero announcement, the August 2026 credit agreements and the September 2026 euro notes, and seven DEF 14A proxy statements (2020-2026). Peer filings used directly: Lyft (FY2019-FY2025 annual and 2024-Q3 through 2026-Q2 quarterly), Grab (20-F FY2021-FY2025), DoorDash (FY2023 and FY2025 annual, 2026-Q2 quarterly), Maplebear, DiDi's final 20-F, C.H. Robinson, RXO, XPO and Landstar.

Transcripts and presentations. Thirty earnings-call transcripts covering Q1 2019 through Q2 2026 without a gap, and 46 conference and special-call transcripts including the February 2022 analyst and investor day, the February 2024 investor update, the July 2026 Delivery Hero acquisition call and the September 2026 Goldman Sachs Communacopia fireside.

Investor presentations. Eleven decks: the 2020 Postmates and 2021 Transplace acquisition decks, six quarterly earnings supplementals from Q3 2021 to Q2 2026, the 189-slide 2022 Investor Day, the 82-slide February 2024 Investor Update, and the July 2026 Delivery Hero announcement deck. The 2022 Investor Day PDF contains no extractable text across all 189 pages.

Market data. Bloomberg terminal pulls dated 21 and 22 September 2026: daily price, high, low, total-return index, price-to-book and market capitalisation since the May 2019 IPO; weekly one- and two-year-forward consensus EPS, P/E, sales and EBITDA since listing; annual actuals FY2016-FY2025 and BEst consensus FY2025-FY2029; twelve quarters of actual-against-consensus with next-session price reactions; each quarter's guide against the consensus already published for the guided quarter; and a 36-row comparable-company table. Cross-sectional base rates were built from a 28-ticker consumer-marketplace panel and a 518-ticker S&P 500 plus Nasdaq-100 panel covering FY2000-FY2025, 46,189 non-null observations.

Derived series. A ten-year annual financial history and a twelve-quarter series reconciled line by line to the filings; a driver-based operating model with 26 drivers across three scenarios and a one-at-a-time sensitivity; a per-segment peer scale and KPI comparison for ride-hail, delivery and freight brokerage; a monthly buyback record against the price paid; and a thirty-three-year debt and restricted-asset history.

Gaps and failures. No sell-side coverage of Uber exists in the local digest, so every external expectation here is Bloomberg consensus or cited press. Six SQLite data stores were unavailable. No year-over-year 10-K redline exists for Uber, so risk-factor changes come from Item 1A of all seven annual reports. Bloomberg publishes no consensus for Gross Bookings, gross merchandise value, MAPCs, Trips, Uber One members, Delivery advertising, insurance expense or any segment line, and returns no estimate high, low or standard-deviation fields for this ticker, so dispersion here uses contributor counts and the published high-to-low span. Bloomberg's EBITDA series exceeds an income-statement-derived EBITDA by $287M to $480M a year from FY2019 onward and the difference is unexplained. No Delivery Hero primary financial statement is used, so every figure in the Delivery Hero block comes from Uber's own acquisition deck and the pending-acquisition note. DiDi deregistered from the SEC after its 2021 delisting and files nothing, so every DiDi figure is press reporting of a results announcement. Bolt, Ola, Rapido, inDrive and Gojek's ride-hail business file nothing. Just Eat Takeaway.com and Deliveroo return no current market data after their acquisitions and their comparable-table rows are blank.

Discrepancy log. Twelve items where two sources disagree, resolved as follows. FY2018 and FY2019 revenue exists on two bases, $11,270M and $14,147M in the FY2019 annual report against $10,433M and $13,000M after the Q4 2020 presentation change; the restated basis is used throughout and any take-rate series spanning 2019 depends on which is chosen. Bloomberg holds pre-restatement revenue for FY2016 and FY2017 and post-restatement from FY2018, so a Bloomberg-sourced revenue series has a break at that boundary. FY2023 accrued insurance reserves are $2,015M in the FY2023 filing and $2,230M in the FY2025 filing. Uber's recast non-GAAP EPS for Q2 and Q3 2025 is $0.60 and $0.65, Bloomberg's comparable-adjusted actual is $0.637 and $0.683, and Bloomberg's contemporaneous consensus was $0.838 and $0.911. The all-time high is $100.10 on a closing basis and $101.99 intraday, two weeks apart, so "down X% from the high" differs by about two points depending on which is used. Freight Gross Bookings does not equal Freight revenue despite the stated definition, with the gap widening from about $1M a quarter to $12M. Total debt is $10,600M of principal and $10,521M on the balance sheet at December 2025, the difference being unamortised discount and issuance costs. Bloomberg's return on invested capital of 34.4% and 35.2% for FY2024 and FY2025 rises on the valuation-allowance releases and is not an operating return; the figures here are rebuilt from operating income. FY2024 Delivery revenue is $13,748M in one filing and $13,750M in the next. DoorDash's FY2021 Marketplace gross order value is $41,944M in its FY2023 annual report against a $43,127M shareholder-letter figure, and the filed number is used, which widens both the share loss and the growth gap. RXO's Coyote purchase price is $1,048M final and not the $1,025M sometimes quoted. And the Transplace consideration is described as all-cash in the annual report and as $1.5bn cash plus $750M of stock in the announcement deck.

Internal discrepancies. Twelve quantities appear at two values or on two bases inside this document, and nothing here settles them.

  • Return on invested capital for FY2023-FY2025 is 9.0%, 22.5% and 41.1% in Section 3, which shows the build on average invested capital, and 9.1%, 20.9% and 40.7% in Section 13.1 on the same stated basis. Section 3's series is the one used elsewhere, including the peer table.
  • The FY2025 Delivery order count is a 3.4-4.6bn working band in Section 1.2, the 2.8-3.8bn residual angle in the Section 4.2 peer table, and 2.8-4.6bn in Section 20, and average order value moves with it, $19.75-$26.72 against $24-$32.
  • In the Section 1.3 Freight table the Other cost column is on the Adjusted EBITDA basis in the annual rows, $549M for FY2025, and on the Segment Operating Income basis in the two quarterly rows, $154M, which annualises to $616M. The decline from $595M to $549M and the flat $154M are not one measure.
  • The unallocated corporate line on the Segment Operating Income basis is $4,686M for FY2025 in Sections 13.3 and 17.1, 73% above the retired measure's $2,708M, against $(907)M to $(1,077)M a quarter and about 50% larger in Appendix A. The $4,686M figure is what Section 17 models.
  • FY2025 share repurchases are $6,523M in the cash-flow lines of Sections 10.6 and 13.2 and $6,560M in the monthly price-paid record, and Q2 2026 is $510M against $518M.
  • Q2 2026 investment gains are $1.3bn in the reading notes at the front and a $1.6bn pre-tax net revaluation benefit in Section 18.
  • The assumed autonomous-vehicle price is $50,000-$60,000 in Section 14 and $70,000-$80,000 in Section 18, which is $6.0-7.2bn against $8.4-9.6bn for the same 120,000 vehicles. Section 20 uses the union of the two.
  • Section 17.2 treats the Section 17.5 sensitivities as one-sided moves when each is a bear-to-bull swing. The $6.0bn attributed there to cutting Gross Bookings per Mobility trip from +2.5% to +0.5% is about $3.0bn on the table's own construction, and the $2.2bn attributed to a Mobility net take of 19.5% reconciles with neither reading.
  • Delivery Hero FY2025 revenue is $16,576M in Section 4.2 and $15,893M in Section 17.2, and Meituan FY2025 revenue growth is 8.1% in Section 3.2 and 8.3% in Section 17.2.
  • C.H. Robinson's FY2025 margin appears as 16.8% in Section 3.3, on whole-company adjusted gross profit, and as 14.8% in Section 4.3, on North American brokerage net revenue. The widening gap in Section 3.3 depends on the first basis.
  • Insurance reserves at the end of FY2022 are $4,720M in Section 12.5 and $4,754M in Section 18.
  • Section 17.4 states that the base share path is affordable at any repurchase price between $75 and $110 through FY2030. At $110 even the low end of that path, 68M shares, is $7.5bn against $5.3bn of half of base FY2026 free cash flow.

Corrections. Uber introduced Non-GAAP Operating Income, Non-GAAP Net Income and Non-GAAP EPS with the Q4 2025 release on 4 February 2026, recasting quarters back to Q1 2024, one quarter earlier and two years deeper than the segment-measure change that followed in Q1 2026. Uber Freight's estimated quarterly load count is 640,000 to 785,000, and the count coincides across the two quarters compared only at the contract-brokerage price. Mobility's net take of 20.7% in Q2 2026 compares with a disclosed 2018 Ridesharing Take Rate of 21%; the 20% figure sometimes quoted from the IPO prospectus is the Core Platform blend of ridesharing at 21% and Uber Eats at 10%. The 2020 Freight Series A investor was one of two outside financial investors in Uber Freight: the Public Investment Fund bought Series A preferred representing 4% fully diluted in July 2021, and no Uber filing names Greenbriar. And the FY2016 figure of $2,876M is income from discontinued operations after tax, not the gain on the Uber China disposal, which was $6,219M pre-tax.

Estimates by method. Twenty-two figures here are tagged [estimate: …] and each states its bounds. Six are residual or triangulation estimates of an undisclosed unit count: Mobility trips and Delivery orders from the platform trip total, Delivery advertising revenue from a build-forward and a penetration anchor, Freight loads from two external per-load price benchmarks, Instacart's order count, and US Mobility trips from a geographic build. Four are cost-allocation estimates: Uber's unallocated corporate bucket spread across segments on three bases, the insurance share of the Mobility cost dollar, the payments share of an incremental booking dollar, and the AV vehicle capital per trip. Four are restatement estimates that put two companies on one basis: DoorDash's gross order value ex-tips, Uber Delivery fully loaded for corporate cost, Uber's implied Gross Bookings from consensus revenue at a revenue-margin band, and Mobility's US share against Lyft. Three are scale estimates from partial disclosure: Bolt's ride-hail bookings, Trendyol GO's contribution to FY2025 Delivery growth, and Waymo's share of Uber's top-20-city volume. Three are cost-of-capital or loaded-cost estimates: the value of the September 2026 headcount reduction, the equal-dollar buyback benchmark, and the lease discount-rate sensitivity. Two are refinancing estimates: the 2028 maturity step-up and the Delivery Hero acquisition interest.

Web sources. Roughly forty distinct domains are cited, concentrated in five groups: company investor-relations pages and press releases for DoorDash, J.B. Hunt, C.H. Robinson, RXO and Grab; trade and business press for autonomy and delivery competition, principally CNBC, TechCrunch, Caixin Global, FreightWaves and Investing.com; regulator and industry publications, principally the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission, Transport Topics and Armstrong & Associates; legal and tax commentary on the UK VAT judgment; and Uber's own engineering and newsroom pages. Every web-sourced claim in the body is quoted verbatim in Appendix B. Two claims are marked [web, unverified] because their pages could not be re-fetched: the Q2 2026 consensus figures behind that quarter's price reaction, and Delivery Hero's regional share of group EBITDA.

External datasets. None were collected. Appendix C lists the two that are available for a business of this shape and what each would test.

20. What we still don't know, and the metrics that would resolve it

Ten gaps are material enough to change a conclusion. Each is stated as something not known about Uber, and each names the disclosure or series that would close it.

1. How many Mobility trips and how many Delivery orders. Uber reports Trips only as the two combined, 13,567M in FY2025 and 3,867M in Q2 2026. Two independent builds put Delivery orders between 2.8bn and 4.6bn, a spread of about two-thirds, and every per-trip and per-order figure in Section 1, every unit-economics line, and the Mobility trip-growth driver that decides the model depend on the split. Resolves with: a disclosed Mobility trip count or Delivery order count in any period; failing that, an order-count and basket panel from a card or app engagement source.

2. The level of Delivery advertising revenue. Only the year-over-year dollar change is disclosed. The estimate of $1.7-2.0bn for FY2025 supports the conclusion that roughly half of Delivery's segment profit is a media business and 1.8 of the 5.70 points of the model's FY2027 Delivery incremental margin. It is biased high because the Q4 2023 base figure was company-wide advertising including a Mobility format. Resolves with: an advertising revenue level by segment, or the penetration figure as a disclosure instead of an analyst's premise that management accepted.

3. How much of the Mobility margin gain is favourable reserve development. Insurance reserves were $12,463M at December 2025 and $13,286M at June 2026, they are a critical audit matter, and prior-year development is recognised in current-year results, so a margin move can be a reserve revision instead of an operating change. Mobility Segment Operating Income rose 28% in Q2 2026 and 167bp of the gain came out of the cost line that contains insurance. Uber discloses the change in insurance expense and never the level. Resolves with: a reserve roll-forward separating current-year additions from prior-year development, or the statutory annual statements of the captive and of Uber's ridesharing carriers, which include loss-development triangles and earned premium.

4. How much of consumer growth is acquired. MAPCs went 171M to 202M to 208M across the window in which Uber closed Trendyol GO in June 2025, SpotHero in April 2026 and Getir in July 2026. Uber does not split revenue into organic and acquired and does not split MAPCs at all. Trendyol GO alone books at about $10 an order against a $20-30 blend, so acquired consumers arrive with a different frequency and a different value per transaction. Resolves with: an organic MAPC or Gross Bookings figure, or the acquired businesses sized on either metric.

5. What an AV partner pays Uber. No party discloses the AV software licence or the commercial terms of an AV trip: whether Uber earns a commission comparable to a human trip, a fixed platform fee, or a fleet-operations margin. That single number determines whether the model's Mobility net cut of 20.15% in FY2033 is conservative or optimistic, and it is the difference between the bear case at 18.70% and the bull at 21.20%. Resolves with: an AV revenue, take-rate or contribution disclosure, or AV trips reported as a level instead of a percentage.

6. Where the $10bn of AV investment lands, and when. There is no disclosed split between capitalised vehicle purchases, equity investments in software partners and operating expense, and no disclosed timing. Consensus models $2,300M of cumulative capex across four years against management's own arithmetic of $6.0-9.6bn of vehicles alone. A ±$1.0bn annual move is worth $2,000M of FY2033 free cash flow. Resolves with: a cash requirement in the purchase-commitments note, or a named fleet-financing vehicle with a stated balance-sheet treatment.

7. Delivery Hero's own balance sheet. The target's net debt is never stated in Uber's disclosure and its convertible bonds are never mentioned. A change-of-control put on those converts would sit on top of the €14.2bn bridge and the €4.0bn term loan, against a commitment to hold gross leverage below 2x and keep an investment-grade rating. Uber's own funding plan states that repayment depends partly on Delivery Hero's balance sheet. Resolves with: Delivery Hero's IFRS annual report and half-year interim, and the BaFin offer document published 27 August 2026.

8. The net operating loss balance and the cash-tax path. The $6.4bn US and $5.0bn Netherlands valuation-allowance releases created $10,951M of net deferred tax assets at December 2025, and no carryforward balance, expiry schedule or jurisdiction mix is reflected in the cash-tax projection, which ramps from $(671)M in FY2025 to $(5,700)M in FY2033 and is second only to segment profit itself on the terminal free-cash-flow build. The £1.4bn of HMRC VAT already paid under protest is a separate cash item outside that path. Resolves with: the income-tax footnote's carryforwards by jurisdiction with expiry, run against the projected pre-tax income path.

9. Whether the 2026 growth acceleration is structural or a soft comparison. Gross Bookings growth of +24% in Q2 2026 against +19% for FY2025 is the single most-cited fact in the current numbers, and Q2 2025 grew 17% against FY2024's 18.1%, which is consistent with a soft quarter creating an easy comparison. Q4 is the seasonal high for both Mobility and Delivery and Q1 the low, and no two-year stacked comparison across the eight quarters to Q2 2026 exists to separate the comp effect from the acceleration. Resolves with: a two-year stacked growth series, or management quantifying the seasonal and comparison effects.

10. Whether there is customer, merchant, advertiser or shipper concentration. Uber discloses that no customer accounted for 10% or more of consolidated revenue and that "A significant amount of our Delivery Gross Bookings come from a limited number of large restaurant groups and other merchants", without a figure. Three businesses inside the company are enterprise-contracted — advertising, where enterprise growth now outpaces small-business growth; Uber Direct's retail-chain clients; and Freight, serving more than 100 Fortune 500 shippers — and none has a named-customer or top-ten disclosure. Resolves with: a merchant, advertiser or shipper concentration disclosure of the kind C.H. Robinson gives, which reports its top 100 customers at 40% of consolidated revenue.

Four further gaps do not change a conclusion but narrow one. Uber's earner supply is known as a price and never as a quantity: there is no disclosure of driver churn, driver earnings per hour, the eligible pool or its outside option, and the mechanism that would reverse the declining incentive spend the model assumes persists runs through exactly those variables. Uber publishes revenue by geography for all three segments combined and nothing by segment or by country over time, so the consolidated Revenue Margin decline from 27.6% in FY2022 to 26.9% in FY2025 cannot be separated into geographic mix and pricing, and the fastest-growing region, EMEA at 31.5% of revenue after growing 65% in two years, is where the UK change, Careem, Trendyol GO, Getir, Delivery Hero and most live driver-classification rulings all land. Mobility's non-ride adjacencies — carshare, rentals, transit ticketing, Uber for Business, Uber Health, driver financial products and SpotHero parking — are named in the 10-K and sized nowhere, and they book at different values per transaction inside a per-trip denominator. And segment assets are not reported at all, so no segment return on capital is computable, which matters most for Mobility as autonomy moves it toward vehicle capital.

Monitoring metrics, in the order they would turn. Monthly trips per MAPC, which grew +2% in Q2 2026, the lowest of the last five quarters. MAPC growth, which went 18%, 17%, 16%. The gap between Gross Bookings growth and trip growth, which opened to about six points in Q2 2026, two of them currency. Mobility Segment Operating Income as a percentage of Gross Bookings, where reinvested insurance savings and AV partner economics land first. Driver and courier payments and incentives inside cost of revenue, where a supply-cost war shows up. Insurance expense returning as a named increase in the cost-of-revenue discussion. Delivery Gross Bookings growth against DoorDash's organic rate. Uber One member growth and the member share of Gross Bookings. Waymo's published weekly ride count, the only externally observable AV volume series. And the accrued-insurance-reserve line in the cash-flow statement, which is the difference between free cash flow growing with profit and free cash flow growing at 7.5%.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Eleven decks span the July 2020 Postmates announcement through the August 2026 quarterly supplemental. They matter disproportionately for this company because several of the numbers that decide the analysis appear only there: per-segment contribution margin, long-term segment margin targets, a country-level profitability distribution, an advertising revenue level, and the demand-variability ratios underneath the autonomy argument.

What the decks add

  • The segment cost breakdown, published once. In the top-20 markets already at or above target margin in Q4 2021, driver payments took 73% of Mobility Gross Bookings, insurance and payments 4%, technology and support 2%, and acquisition, retention and engagement 5%, leaving 15% contribution and 13% Adjusted EBITDA after 2% of fixed cost. The Delivery version: driver and merchant payments 82%, insurance and payments 1%, technology and support 3%, acquisition and engagement 6%, for 8% contribution and 6% Adjusted EBITDA [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 179]. The word "contribution" does not appear in the FY2025 10-K. Informs §1.
  • The long-term segment margin targets management is measured against. Mobility 25% revenue take rate times a 45% Adjusted EBITDA margin gives 11.25% of Gross Bookings; Delivery 15% times 30% gives 4.50%; total company 7.00% of Gross Bookings▪ [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 177]. Q2 2026 actuals are 7.6% and 3.8% on the stricter Segment Operating Income basis, and Delivery has taken four more points of the basket than it planned while converting ten fewer points of it into profit. Informs §1 and §3.
  • Market-level profitability. In FY2023, 85% of the top-ten countries were profitable in each segment, Mobility's top ten ran at 7% of Gross Bookings and Delivery's top ten at 2%, with the majority still below best-in-class [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slide 71]. Informs §1 and §3.
  • Cross-platform economics in dollar levels. Quarterly platform Gross Bookings per consumer in Q4 2021 were $58 for Mobility-only, $151 for Delivery-only and $364 for cross-platform [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 114]. The 10-K gives only the "over three times" ratio. Informs §3.
  • The cross-app acquisition advantage, and its narrowing. 2.1x the Delivery consumers of all paid channels combined at 25% of paid-channel cost at Q4 2021 [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 111]; 50% of paid-channel cost at FY2023 [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slide 9]; "more than 50% lower" in July 2026 [deck: M&A Announcement Delivery Hero 2026-07-16, slide 9]. The advantage roughly halved between 2021 and 2023. Informs §3.
  • The demand-variability argument against an AV-only competitor. A typical Monday is about 45% of a Saturday and daily troughs about 5% of peaks in the Austin AV operating zone, with AVs as fixed base-load supply and human drivers as boost supply [deck: Q4 2025 earnings supplement 2026-02-04, slide 8]. The ratios are falsifiable; the conclusion drawn from them is Uber's. Informs §1 and §3.
  • The geographic bound on the AV threat. Uber operates in more than 8,000 US markets covering about 95% of the population, and trips originating and ending inside the top 20 US cities are only about 30% of US Mobility Gross Bookings and about 25% of US Mobility profits [deck: Q4 2025 earnings supplement 2026-02-04, slide 9]. Informs §4 and §6.
  • The advertising business in levels. $11M of revenue in FY2020 and $141M in FY2021 against a $1bn-plus target for 2024 [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 137]; by Q4 2023, 170,000 active advertisers in 30-plus countries at 11x average return on ad spend and about $900M annualised, with ads plus merchant-funded offers at about 5% of Delivery Gross Bookings and above 10% in the best country [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slides 39 and 49]. This deck series is the only place a level exists. Informs §1 and §3.
  • Delivery's margin levers, measured. Between Q4 2021 and Q4 2023, consumer incentives declined about 200bp as a share of Gross Bookings, courier cost per trip declined 5% in constant currency, operating costs declined about 200bp, and net consumer fees as a percentage of basket declined 420bp while incomplete trips declined about 25%, worth more than $500M of annualised Gross Bookings [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slides 40 and 45]. Informs §1.
  • The Mobility barbell, quantified. Low-cost products produce 75% higher frequency than standard-only users, premium products 3.5x the profit dollars, and together they drive more than 25% of first-time Mobility users [deck: Q1 2026 earnings supplement 2026-05-06, slide 7]. Informs §1 and §3.
  • What Transplace was. Founded 2000, 3,100 employees, 1,700 customers, 96% gross retention in 2020, average managed-transportation tenure of 8-9 years on 3-5 year contracts, freight under management from $7bn in 2018 to $15bn in 2021, 2021 EBITDA above $100M, bought for $2.25bn with $40M-plus of net run-rate synergies promised in 12-24 months and Uber Freight Adjusted EBITDA breakeven promised by Q4 2022 [deck: Uber Freight acquisition of Transplace 2021-07-22, slides 5-8 and 16]. The 10-K discloses the price and the goodwill and none of the operating detail. Informs §11.
  • Autonomy ranked above buybacks. The February 2024 framework was growth, liquidity, return of capital [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slide 75]; the July 2026 framework is organic growth, autonomous, selective M&A, return excess capital, investment grade [deck: M&A Announcement Delivery Hero 2026-07-16, slide 13]. Autonomy did not exist as a line item in 2024 and now ranks second. Informs §10.
  • The free-cash-flow reconciliation and the captive insurer. Adjusted EBITDA converts to free cash flow through changes in insurance reserves accrued per mile as trips complete, with the cash restricted and unavailable for daily operations but earning investment income, then interest and cash taxes, working capital and capital expenditure [deck: Investor Update 2024-02-14, slides 73-74]. The 10-K discloses the reserve balance and not the reconciliation. Informs §10 and §12.
  • Delivery's addressable market was redefined, not grown. $1.8tn of restaurant spend plus $2.5tn of grocery in 2022 [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 52] against about $2tn of food plus about $10tn of grocery and retail in 2025 [deck: Q3 2025 earnings supplement 2025-11-04, slide 7]. The 2025 figure adds retail, pets, electronics, home and beauty, so a comparison across the two decks is a definitional artefact. Informs §4 and §6.
  • The price ladder autonomy has to beat. Average US price per trip in 2019 was $48 for Uber Black, $16 for UberX and $12 for UberX Share, against about $2 for public transport at 191M weekly trips, 7x Uber's volume, and about $0.50 per mile for personal vehicles at 6.6bn weekly trips [deck: Investor Day 2022-02-10, slide 39]. The competitor autonomy has to displace is the private car. Informs §4 and §6.

The decks expose three measurement breaks. The segment measure change is worth $176M for Mobility, $110M for Delivery and $18M for Freight in a single quarter, so a chart running Segment Adjusted EBITDA to 2025 and Segment Operating Income from 2026 shows a step-down of roughly 0.6 points of Mobility Gross Bookings that did not happen. The unallocated corporate bucket is about 50% larger on the new measure, at $(907)M to $(1,077)M a quarter against $(632)M to $(683)M on the old one. And cross-platform penetration is quoted on at least four different populations — 17% of active consumers at Q4 2021, a third of monthly consumers multi-product at Q4 2023, about 40% of eligible Uber One members across both in Q2 2026, and about one in five eligible consumers in the FY2025 10-K.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets fit a business of this shape. Neither was collected, and both would test quantities Uber does not disclose.

Google Trends — relative search interest. What it is: an index of search volume for a brand or product term over time, available weekly and by country and region. What it measures: the direction and seasonality of consumer intent toward Uber and toward each named competitor, independent of anything the company reports. How it would inform this analysis: the Mobility and Delivery consumer counts are the top node of both driver trees in §1, and Uber reports only a single combined MAPC figure with no organic-versus-acquired split and no geographic breakdown, so a brand-interest series by country is the cheapest independent check on whether the 2026 consumer acceleration is Uber or the category. The same series against Lyft, Bolt, DoorDash, Keeta and iFood would test the share statements in §4, where Uber's own category-position metric is internally computed and not independently verified. The index is relative, so it shows direction and turning points and gives no levels. It was not collected.

App and web engagement panels — downloads, daily and monthly active users, time spent, churn. What it is: third-party measurement of mobile app installs, active-user counts, session frequency and retention, assembled from device panels and store data. What it measures: consumer adoption and repeat use, split by app, country and cohort. How it would inform this analysis: two quantities constrain the analysis more than any others and both are exactly what these panels price. The Mobility-versus-Delivery volume split is estimated in §1 and §13 from an assumed Delivery average order value, with two independent builds disagreeing by about a third on the Delivery order level, and a separate active-user and session series for the Rides and Eats apps would narrow it. And monthly trips per MAPC is the only frequency disclosure Uber gives, at +2% in Q2 2026, with no churn, no cohort retention and no split between new and returning consumers, so a retention panel would separate the frequency gain from the consumer additions in §6's growth attribution and test the membership lock in §3. A download series by market would also size the cross-platform conversion rate that has been stuck near one in five for several years. These figures are assembled from scattered cited points instead of a single vendor feed, so any series built this way is a partial mosaic and not a comprehensive measurement. It was not collected.

Neither dataset would resolve the level of Delivery advertising revenue, because it is a merchant-side price and these panels measure consumer behaviour. The nearest substitute is a merchant advertising-spend or sponsored-listing pricing panel, which is not among the sources available here.
